questions.why: Qwest did this in 1999, adding about a fifth of that year’s profit. Later restatements showed revenues overstated by $2.2 billion.

questions.q: Graham found that the four companies’ P/E ratios varied far more than their operating performance or financial condition did.
questions.why: ELTRA and Emhart sold at about 10 and 12 times earnings; Emerson and Emery at 33 and 45, though all four performed well.

questions.q: Graham thought Emery Air Freight’s price of more than 60 times recent earnings was justified for the careful investor.
questions.why: Maybe for someone with an in-depth study and exceptionally firm conclusions, he says, but not for the careful investor wary of Wall Street’s overenthusiasm.

questions.q: Graham measures stability by the largest fall in EPS in any of the past ten years, compared with the average of the three years before it.
questions.why: No decline at all means 100% stability. ELTRA and Emhart each fell only about 8% in the poor year of 1970.

questions.q: Graham’s standard for a manufacturing company is at least R2 of current assets for every R1 of current liabilities.
questions.why: The three manufacturers met it. Emery, a service business with a fine record, had a lower ratio but could easily raise cash.

questions.q: ELTRA and Emhart both met Graham’s seven statistical requirements for a defensive investor’s portfolio.
questions.why: Both sold close to book value with satisfactory returns on capital, stability and growth: reasonably protected investments.

questions.q: Graham would have advised holders of Emerson and Emery to switch at once into ELTRA and Emhart, expecting them to do better within months.
questions.why: There was no reason to expect quick outperformance, since popular shares can keep their momentum. The switch makes sense only for someone who prefers value to glamour.

questions.q: Zweig argues that a 2-for-1 share split makes shareholders richer, since they now own twice as many shares.
questions.why: Two nickels are not worth more than one dime. A split doubles the shares and halves the price, so the value is unchanged.

questions.q: Two of Graham’s seven tests are a price of no more than 1.5 times net asset value and no more than 15 times average earnings of the past three years.
questions.why: These are his price limits for the defensive investor. The others cover size, finances, dividends, earnings stability and growth.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of Graham’s seven requirements for the defensive investor?
options: A strong share-price trend over the past year
No earnings deficit in the past ten years
Dividends paid for at least the past 20 years
Ten-year growth in EPS of at least one-third
questions.why: Price momentum is for speculators. His tests concern size, finances, dividends, earnings stability, growth and the price paid.

questions.q: Why does Graham suggest that Emery’s spectacular past growth may mean less for its future?
options: It began from a very small base, and high growth is much harder once profits are large
Its accounts were unreliable, so the reported growth may never have happened at all
It paid no dividends, so shareholders saw none of the growth in their own pockets
Air freight was a shrinking industry, so the company’s growth was bound to reverse soon
questions.why: Net earnings were only $570,000 in 1958. Size itself makes a repeat performance more difficult.

questions.q: What point does Graham make by comparing Emerson Electric with Zenith Radio?
options: High valuations carry high risks: Zenith had a brilliant record too, until its profits halved and its share slumped
Emerson would certainly fail as Zenith did, because the two companies operated in the same market
Radio and electronics companies are poor investments, since their products go out of date so quickly
Large companies hardly ever lose much of their value, so Emerson’s size made it far safer than Zenith had been
questions.why: Zenith also reached about $1.7 billion in market value. Then its profits halved and its share fell from 89 to 22½.

questions.q: Analysts may prefer Emerson and Emery for their better “market action” and faster recent growth. How does Graham treat these two reasons?
options: Market action is not a valid reason for a conservative investor; faster growth is valid only within limits
Both are excellent reasons, since price momentum and fast growth tend to go on together for years
Both are irrelevant, since a conservative investor should look only at assets and dividends
Market action is a valid reason, since prices reflect what insiders know, but growth is never a reason
questions.why: Price momentum is “something for the speculators to play around with”. Growth counts, but not at any price.

questions.q: What did Zweig find when he removed EMC’s 1999 acquisition of Data General from its revenue?
options: Its existing business grew only about 3.6%, almost nothing
Its growth was even faster than the 24% it had reported
It had no revenue from data storage at all before the deal
Its profits doubled, even though its revenue barely moved
questions.why: Revenue appeared to jump 24%, but most came from the purchase. At 103 times earnings, the market was paying for growth that wasn’t there.

questions.q: Graham warned that today’s investor “is so concerned with anticipating the future that he is already paying handsomely for it in advance”. What follows?
options: Even if the forecast comes true, he may make no profit, and if it falls short he may suffer a serious loss
Accurate forecasts bring large profits, so the investor should spend more effort on forecasting
Forecasting is unnecessary, because the market price already tells him everything he needs
Paying for growth in advance is usually cheap, since the growth arrives sooner than people expect it to
questions.why: When the price already assumes the good future, getting the future right is not enough. This is the core risk of glamour shares.

questions.q: A share trades at R66 and its book value per share is R10.34. What is its price-to-book ratio, and does it pass Graham’s 1.5-times test?
options: About 6.4 times: it fails
About 1.5 times: it just passes
About 0.16 times: it passes
About 3 times: it fails
questions.why: R66 ÷ R10.34 ≈ 6.4. That was Emerson Electric in 1970, far above Graham’s limit.

questions.q: A company earns R2.70 a share on a book value of R27.05 a share. What is its return on book value?
options: About 10%
About 27%
About 2.7%
About 1%
questions.why: R2.70 ÷ R27.05 ≈ 10%. That was ELTRA: satisfactory, but well below Emerson’s 22% and Emery’s 34.5%.

questions.q: A share trades at R33 with net asset value of R27 a share and three-year average EPS of R2.81. Does it pass both of Graham’s price tests?
options: Yes: about 1.2 times net assets and about 11.7 times earnings
No: at about 1.2 times net assets it fails the asset test
No: at about 11.7 times earnings it fails the earnings test
No: it fails both the asset test and the earnings test
questions.why: R33 ÷ R27 ≈ 1.22 (limit 1.5) and R33 ÷ R2.81 ≈ 11.7 (limit 15). This is roughly Emhart at the end of 1970.

questions.q: A company’s average EPS is now R1.30, against R1.00 ten years ago. Does it meet Graham’s ten-year growth test?
options: No: 30% is short of the required one-third
Yes: any growth over ten years is enough
Yes: 30% is close enough to one-third
No: it needs 100% growth over ten years
questions.why: The test asks for at least a 33⅓% increase in per-share earnings over ten years, measured with three-year averages at each end.

questions.q: A company has current assets of R20.4m and current liabilities of R11.8m. How does its current ratio compare with Graham’s standard for a manufacturer?
options: About 1.7 to 1, below the 2-to-1 standard
About 2.7 to 1, comfortably above the standard
Exactly 2 to 1, which meets the standard
About 0.6 to 1, far below the standard
questions.why: R20.4m ÷ R11.8m ≈ 1.73. That was Emery Air Freight, which Graham excused as a different kind of business.

questions.q: You own 100 shares at R100 each. The company splits its shares 2-for-1. What do you own afterwards?
options: 200 shares at about R50: the same R10,000
200 shares at R100: R20,000
100 shares at R200
200 shares at R60, because splits lift prices
questions.why: A split changes the number of slices, not the size of the cake. Zweig likens it to swapping a dime for two nickels.

questions.q: A company starts the year with R156m in cash, raises R1.3bn in new financing, and ends the year with R1.0bn. Roughly how much cash did its business consume?
options: About R456m
About R1.0bn
About R156m
Nothing: cash rose
questions.why: R156m + R1,300m − R1,000m ≈ R456m. That was Exodus in 1999: rising cash can hide a business devouring money.

questions.q: Using Graham’s growth formula from Chapter 11 (multiplier = 8.5 + 2 × growth), what annual growth does a P/E of 45 imply?
options: About 18%
About 45%
About 10%
About 27%
questions.why: 45 = 8.5 + 2g gives g ≈ 18.25% a year for seven to ten years: a demanding rate to sustain from a large base.

questions.q: Graham says the simplest approach for the defensive investor is to buy equal amounts of each of the 30 shares in the Dow.
questions.why: That gives a true cross-section of leading companies. Zweig notes a low-cost total-market index fund now does the job even better.

questions.q: Graham’s minimum size for an industrial company in the defensive portfolio is $50 million of total assets.
questions.why: For an industrial company it is at least $100 million of annual sales. The $50 million of total assets is his minimum for a public utility.

questions.q: Besides a 2-to-1 current ratio, Graham requires that an industrial company’s long-term debt not exceed its net current assets.
questions.why: Net current assets, or working capital, are current assets minus current liabilities. Both parts make up his test of financial strength.

questions.q: Graham’s earnings-stability test allows a company to report a loss in up to three of the past ten years.
questions.why: He asks for some earnings for the ordinary shares in each of the past ten years: no deficits at all.

questions.q: Graham found the financial-strength tests the most severe of his criteria under the conditions of his time.
questions.why: Many large, formerly strong companies had weakened their current ratio, overexpanded their debt, or both.

questions.q: For public-utility shares, Graham keeps the 2-to-1 current-ratio test but drops the dividend test.
questions.why: He drops the current-ratio test, because utilities finance growth continuously through bonds and shares. He requires adequate equity relative to debt instead.

questions.q: On selling a share that has risen too far, Graham says it is better to sell and pay the tax than not sell and repent.
questions.why: Even defensive portfolios should be changed from time to time when holdings look excessively priced and better-value replacements exist.

questions.q: Zweig considers the “forward” P/E, based on next year’s forecast earnings, the most reliable way to judge a share’s price.
questions.why: He calls it nonsensical to divide a known price by unknown future earnings. Use price ÷ the average of the past three years’ actual earnings.

questions.q: Zweig points out that Graham’s growth test, a third more EPS over ten years, works out to less than 3% a year.
questions.why: He calls it a very low hurdle and suggests 50% over ten years (about 4% a year) as slightly less conservative.

questions.q: Graham advises the defensive investor to rely on a skilled analyst to pick the best few shares rather than diversify widely.
questions.why: He says to let the choice of “best” shares alone and emphasise diversification. If anyone could pick the best unerringly, diversifying would only lose.

questions.q: What made Penn Central’s 1970 bankruptcy so shocking to the financial world?
options: It had paid dividends for over 120 years, and its share had been near its peak only a year or two earlier
It was a small, obscure company that few investors had heard of, so no one had studied its accounts
It had never paid a dividend, so its shareholders had already lost faith in it years before
It was the first railroad ever to fail, and the industry had been thought immune to bankruptcy
questions.why: Graham later shows how a competent student could have detected its weaknesses in time. More than half of US railroad mileage had been in bankruptcy at some point in 50 years.

questions.q: What is Graham’s suggestion on railroad shares?
options: There’s no compelling reason to own them; buy only when the value is too great to look elsewhere
Avoid them completely and forever, since the industry’s record of bankruptcies speaks for itself
Buy them as a whole class, since railroad shares tend to rise together when the economy recovers
Own them in place of utilities, since both are regulated and pay similar dividends
questions.why: He avoids blanket recommendations and blanket condemnations. Zweig applies the same advice to airline shares.

questions.q: What does an investor who stresses “protection” rather than “prediction” mainly seek?
options: A substantial margin of present value above the market price, able to absorb bad news
Confidence that the company’s earnings will grow fast for many years to come
The share with the strongest and most consistent upward price trend in its sector
The best management team in the industry, whatever price the market is asking for the shares
questions.why: Such an investor needn’t be enthusiastic about long-run prospects, only reasonably confident the business will get along.

questions.q: A hundred analysts are asked to choose the “best” five shares in the Dow. Why does Graham expect their lists to differ widely?
options: Prices already reflect the known facts and opinions, so any preference rests mostly on personal partialities
Most analysts are poorly trained, so their choices are close to random whatever the facts may be
The data available to each analyst differ, since companies brief some analysts more fully than others
Analysts are paid to disagree with one another, so that their firms can sell more research to clients
questions.why: If all analysts agreed one share was best, its price would quickly rise until its advantages were offset.

questions.q: Graham calls the protective approach “quantitative”. What does it emphasise?
options: Measurable relationships between price and earnings, assets and dividends, as in sound bond selection
Prospects, management quality and other intangibles that numbers alone can’t capture
Charts of past price movements and trading volume, which show where prices are heading
The opinions of leading analysts, combined into an average score for each share on the list
questions.why: The predictive approach is the qualitative one. Graham was always committed to getting ample value in concrete, demonstrable terms.

questions.q: As 1972 began, what did Graham see as the central appeal of utility shares for the defensive investor?
options: They sold at a moderate price relative to book value, so he could be a part owner of sound businesses
They had the fastest earnings growth of any group of shares over the previous twenty years
They paid no tax on their profits, so more of their earnings could be paid out as dividends
Their dividends and share prices were guaranteed by the government that regulated them
questions.why: They offered almost as much past growth as the industrials, steadier figures, lower prices relative to earnings and assets, and higher dividends.

questions.q: How does Zweig suggest a defensive investor who enjoys stock-picking should set up a portfolio?
options: Keep about 90% of the share money in an index fund and use about 10% to pick shares
Pick all of the shares personally and avoid index funds, which only match the market
Split the share money 50/50 between index funds and shares chosen personally
Put it all into the ten best-known companies, since familiar names are the safest
questions.why: The index fund is the foundation. Only after that solid core is in place should you experiment at the edges.

questions.q: Zweig suggests checking how much of a company is owned by institutions. What level hints that a share is “overowned”?
options: More than about 60%
More than about 10%
More than about 30%
Less than 60%
questions.why: When big institutions sell, they tend to move in lockstep, with disastrous results for the share, like the Rockettes toppling off the stage at once.

questions.q: By early 2003, many former high-tech darlings had plenty of cash and little or no debt. What lesson does Zweig draw?
options: The best values are often found in shares that were once hot and have since gone cold
Technology shares are safe once they have fallen, because their cash protects them
A defensive investor should buy every share in such a table at once, without analysis
Financial strength no longer matters once a share has fallen far enough in price
questions.why: A defensive investor can prosper by looking patiently through the wreckage of a bear market, using Graham’s strength tests.

questions.q: A share sells at 9 times its three-year average earnings and 2.4 times book value. Does it pass Graham’s price-to-assets test?
options: Yes: 9 × 2.4 = 21.6, within the 22.5 limit, even though book value is above 1.5 times
No: at 2.4 times book value it is above the limit of 1.5, so it fails the test
No: the product of the P/E and price-to-book must be below 15 to pass the test
Yes, but only because the P/E is below 10, which lets any price-to-book pass
questions.why: A low earnings multiplier can justify a higher asset multiplier. Graham’s own example: 9 times earnings and 2.5 times book.

questions.q: A share sells at 12 times three-year average earnings and 2.0 times book value. What is the verdict?
options: Fails: 12 × 2.0 = 24, above 22.5
Passes: its P/E is below 15
Passes: its product is below 30
Passes: 2.0 is close enough to 1.5
questions.why: Each test looks fine on its own terms except book value, and the blended multiplier confirms it is too expensive.

questions.q: High-grade bonds yield 10%. By Graham’s rule that a share portfolio’s earnings yield should be at least the bond rate, what is the highest overall P/E it should have?
questions.why: Earnings yield = 1 ÷ P/E, so 10% means a P/E of 100 ÷ 10 = 10. Graham’s own example: 7.5% bonds gave a maximum of 13.3.

questions.q: An industrial company has current assets of R480m, current liabilities of R220m and long-term debt of R300m. How does it fare on Graham’s financial-strength tests?
options: Passes the current-ratio test (about 2.2 to 1) but fails the debt test: debt exceeds R260m working capital
Passes both tests: the current ratio is about 2.2 to 1, and debt is below total current assets of R480m
Fails both tests: the current ratio is below 2 to 1 and debt is above working capital
Fails the current-ratio test at about 1.5 to 1, but passes the debt test comfortably
questions.why: R480m ÷ R220m ≈ 2.18, and working capital is R480m − R220m = R260m, which is less than the R300m of debt.

questions.q: A utility has R900m of debt and ordinary shareholders’ equity at book value of R400m. Does it meet Graham’s test for utilities?
options: No: debt is 2.25 times equity, above the limit of twice equity
Yes: debt is below R1bn, the limit for a utility of this size
Yes: utilities have no debt limit, since their profits are regulated
No: under Graham’s rules utilities may carry no debt at all
questions.why: R900m ÷ R400m = 2.25. For utilities Graham allows debt of up to twice the stock equity at book value.

questions.q: A company’s EPS was R1.80, R2.10 and R2.10 ten years ago, and R2.50, R2.70 and R2.90 in the last three years. Does it pass Graham’s growth test?
options: Yes: the averages are R2.00 and R2.70, a 35% rise
No: per-share growth is below the required 50%
No: the latest year is only R2.90, below the target
Yes: the last year alone is up 61% on the first
questions.why: Compare three-year averages, not single years: R2.70 ÷ R2.00 = 1.35, above the one-third minimum.

questions.q: A share is R60. Analysts forecast R5 of EPS next year; the past three years averaged R3. What P/E does Graham’s method give, and does it pass?
options: 20 times: it fails the limit of 15
12 times: it passes the limit of 15
15 times: it just passes the limit
5 times: it is very cheap indeed
questions.why: R60 ÷ R3 = 20. The 12 times on forecast earnings is the forward P/E Zweig warns against: 59% of consensus forecasts miss by 15% or more.

questions.q: A share falls 99.5%, as MicroStrategy did from 2000 to 2002. What gain would it need to get back to its old price?
options: About 19,900%: it must rise 200-fold
About 99.5%, the same as the fall
About 995%: it must rise tenfold
About 200%: it must roughly triple
questions.why: What is left is 0.5% of the old price, and 1 ÷ 0.005 = 200 times. Diversification is the only reliable insurance against being wrong.

questions.q: At the end of 1970 the Dow stood at 839, with three-year average earnings of 55.5 and net asset value of 562. How did the average fare on Graham’s price tests?
options: About 15 times earnings and 1.49 times assets: just within both limits
About 10 times earnings and 1.0 times assets: comfortably cheap
About 15 times earnings but 2.5 times assets: fails the asset test
About 20 times earnings and 1.5 times assets: fails the earnings test
questions.why: 839 ÷ 55.5 ≈ 15.1 and 839 ÷ 562 ≈ 1.49. All seven criteria were met in aggregate, two of them only just.

questions.q: Graham reads the funds’ failure to beat a broad average as strong evidence that doing so is extremely difficult.
questions.why: The funds had the best analysts and full research departments, with costs of about half a percent a year. Even so, a 1960–68 study found random portfolios did better.

questions.q: Graham-Newman selected arbitrages and liquidations that offered a calculated annual return of at least 10% and even odds of success.
questions.why: The tests were a calculated return of 20% or more a year, and a judgment that the chance of success was at least four in five.

questions.q: Graham-Newman typically bought net-current-asset issues at two-thirds or less of that stripped-down value, and held at least 100 of them.
questions.why: Plant and other assets were counted as nothing. Wide diversification was part of the method.

questions.q: Graham-Newman kept up “unrelated” hedging because it proved their most dependable source of profit.
questions.why: It was one of two fields they dropped after ten years of results showed the profits weren’t dependable or “headache proof” enough.

questions.q: Graham lets the enterprising investor allow a considerable plus in one factor to offset a small black mark in another.
questions.why: He might not rule out a company with a loss in a year like 1970 if large average earnings and other strengths made the share look cheap.

questions.q: Graham’s screen for the enterprising investor set a minimum company size of $100 million in annual sales.
questions.why: He set no lower limit on size. Small companies can offer enough safety if bought carefully and as a group.

questions.q: In Graham’s tests, 90 randomly chosen shares fell an average of 22% while the S&P composite was practically unchanged.
questions.why: Smaller, inferior issues tend to be overvalued in bull markets, fall harder afterwards and recover slowly, if at all.

questions.q: Graham’s list of “good-will giants”, priced far above book value, did worst of the 20-odd lists he tested.
questions.why: Contrary to his own philosophy, they did best, up 15%. He still preferred shares backed by asset values of at least two-thirds of the price.

questions.q: Graham advised spending about a year tracking and picking shares on paper before using real money.
questions.why: Afterwards, compare your results with an S&P 500 index fund. If you lagged or didn’t enjoy it, stock-picking isn’t for you.

questions.q: In valuing a “bargain issue”, Graham gives no value at all to plant, buildings and other fixed assets.
questions.why: He counts only net current assets after deducting all prior claims. Buying below that leaves the fixed assets as a free extra.

questions.q: Which is one of Graham’s two explanations for why skilled analysts struggle to beat the market?
options: Analysts tend to buy the best-prospect companies at any price and shun weaker ones however cheap
Analysts lack access to company accounts, so they rely on management for nearly all their data
Trading costs are higher for professionals than for amateurs, which eats away their extra returns
Funds are barred from buying smaller companies, which is where most bargains are found
questions.why: The other explanation is that prices already reflect the facts and reasonable expectations, so later moves are largely unpredictable.

questions.q: Why does Graham think analysts’ habit of buying “the best” at any price is flawed?
options: Very few companies sustain high growth for long, and remarkably few large ones go extinct
The best companies pay the highest dividends, so their shares are worth almost any price
Weak companies nearly always recover fully, so the cheapest shares are the safest buys
Prices never reflect a company’s growth, so analysts can always find hidden value in it
questions.why: Most companies’ histories are of ups and downs and changing relative standing, sometimes “rags to riches and back”.

questions.q: What point does Graham make with his duplicate-bridge analogy?
options: When experts are equally skilled and share ideas freely, winners are decided mostly by breaks, not skill
Bridge players make better investors, because both games reward memory and careful counting
Skill always wins in the long run, so the best analysts will beat the market over enough hands
The best analysts work alone and never share their ideas, as bridge experts keep their hands hidden
questions.why: Analysts sharing ideas at get-togethers is like bridge experts looking over each other’s shoulders and arguing out each hand.

questions.q: Which two single-criterion methods does Graham say gave consistently good results over the long past?
options: Low-multiplier shares of important companies, and groups of shares bought below net current assets
High dividend yields, and low prices per share compared with those of other companies in the market
Strong upward price momentum, and the highest quality rankings in the standard investment guides
Large numbers of shares in issue, and low prices relative to the previous year’s highs
questions.why: Even so, the low-multiplier method applied to the Dow at the end of 1968 worked badly up to mid-1971. Bargain issues had no such blot, but became scarce.

questions.q: Following Graham’s philosophy, when would an enterprising investor buy major cyclical companies, such as steel shares?
options: When the situation is unfavourable, near-term prospects are poor and the low price fully reflects the gloom
When earnings are at a record high and the industry’s order books are full for the year ahead
When analysts are most enthusiastic and the shares have started to rise on heavy trading volume
Never: cyclical companies are only for speculators, because their earnings swing too much to value
questions.why: Zweig adds that yesterday’s losers are often tomorrow’s winners.

questions.q: After reviewing three 1971 “workouts” (a rejected merger, a renegotiated cash bid and an uncertain liquidation), what did Graham conclude?
options: They are not attractive if entered into at random; it has become a field for professionals
They are a reliable source of 40% annual returns for anyone who reads the merger news
Every announced merger is a safe bet, since the deals almost always go through as planned
They suit defensive investors best, since the outcome depends on a contract, not on markets
questions.why: An increasing share of announced mergers failed, from antitrust, shareholder opposition and other causes. Zweig says merger arbitrage is wholly inappropriate for most individuals.

questions.q: Where do many of the best professional investors suggest starting the search for promising shares?
options: The daily list of new 52-week lows
The list of the year’s biggest gainers
Shares most recommended by brokers
The most-traded shares of the day
questions.why: Many top investors first get interested in a company when its price goes down, not up: unloved shares can pay off once perceptions change.

questions.q: Complete Buffett’s proverb: “When a management with a reputation for brilliance tackles a business with a reputation for bad economics…”
options: “…it is the reputation of the business that remains intact.”
“…it is the management’s reputation that always wins out.”
“…the share price doubles before the business turns around.”
“…both reputations improve as the business is turned around.”
questions.why: Buffett looks for “franchise” companies with strong brands, simple businesses, sound finances and near-monopolies in their markets.

questions.q: A new CEO arrives. How does one fund manager read heavy turnover among the division heads listed in the annual report?
options: Good in the first year or two (clearing dead wood); a bad sign if it continues
A bad sign from the start, because the new CEO is losing experienced people
A good sign however long it goes on, since fresh managers bring new ideas
Irrelevant to the investment case, since division heads don’t set the strategy
questions.why: If high turnover persists, the turnaround has probably turned into turmoil.

questions.q: What does Zweig say successful professional investors have in common, whatever their technique?
options: They are disciplined and consistent, and pay very little attention to what the market is doing
They change their approach whenever it falls out of fashion, to keep up with the market
They follow the market minute by minute, so that they can act before anyone else does
They all use the same screening method, built on Graham’s tests for defensive investors
questions.why: As Max Heine put it, “there are many roads to Jerusalem”. Consistency and thought matter more than the road chosen.

questions.q: A company has current assets of R500m and total liabilities of R200m, with 10 million shares in issue. At what price would Graham-Newman typically buy?
options: About R20 or less: two-thirds of net current asset value of R30
About R30: the net current asset value of each share itself
About R50: the value of current assets for each share in issue
About R45: one and a half times net current asset value of R30
questions.why: (R500m − R200m) ÷ 10m = R30 a share, after deducting all liabilities, and two-thirds of that is R20. Subtracting only current liabilities is the trap.

questions.q: An acquirer offers 1⅓ of its shares for each target share. The acquirer trades at R26 and the target at R28. What gross profit does buying the target and selling the acquirer lock in, if the deal goes through?
options: About 24%
About 7%
About 33%
Nothing: the prices already match
questions.why: 1⅓ × R26 = R34.67, and (R34.67 − R28) ÷ R28 ≈ 24%. That was Kayser-Roth and Borden in 1971; the board rejected the deal, and unwinding cost about 12%.

questions.q: A company is bid for at R11 a share in cash, and its shares trade at R8.80. What is the gross profit if the bid succeeds?
options: R2.20 a share, or 2.2%
questions.why: (R11 − R8.80) ÷ R8.80 = 25%, before the risks of non-completion and the time it takes.

questions.q: You buy a bargain issue at R20 and receive R53 in a takeover 3½ years later. What is your total profit, and the simple (non-compounded) annual return?
options: 165% in total, about 47% a year
265% in total, about 76% a year
165% in total, about 33% a year
33% in total, about 9% a year
questions.why: (R53 − R20) ÷ R20 = 165%, and 165% ÷ 3.5 ≈ 47%. That was Burton-Dixie: patience was needed, but it paid.

questions.q: A share passes Graham’s P/E screen of 9 or less. Current assets are 1.6 times current liabilities, and debt is 120% of net current assets. Does it pass his financial-condition test for the enterprising investor?
options: No: debt above 110% of net current assets fails, although the current ratio passes
Yes: both parts pass, since the current ratio is above 1.5 and debt is under 150%
No: the current ratio must be at least 2 to 1, even for the enterprising investor
Yes: the P/E is low enough to make up for any weakness in the financial position
questions.why: His looser tests are current assets of at least 1.5 times current liabilities, and debt of no more than 110% of net current assets.

questions.q: A share’s net tangible assets are R25 a share. Under Graham’s enterprising screen, what is the most you should pay?
options: Under R30 (120% of net tangible assets)
Under R37.50 (150% of net tangible assets)
Under R25 (100% of net tangible assets)
Under R16.67 (two-thirds of net tangible assets)
questions.why: R25 × 1.2 = R30. The two-thirds figure applies to Graham-Newman’s net-current-asset bargains, not to this screen.

questions.q: A company has owner earnings of R120m and invested capital of R1bn. How would the fund manager Zweig cites judge its ROIC?
options: 12%: attractive, above the 10% mark
12%: too low, below the 20% mark
8.3%: unattractive, below the 10% mark
120%: impossible, so recheck it
questions.why: R120m ÷ R1,000m = 12%. Even 6% or 7% can tempt if the company has good brands or focused management, or is under a temporary cloud.

questions.q: You appraise a business at R50 a share. One manager likes “60-cent dollars”. What is the most he would pay?
questions.why: 60% of R50 is R30. Buying at 60% or less of appraised value supplies Graham’s margin of safety.

questions.q: After a year of picking shares on paper, your portfolio is up 8% while an index fund rose 12%. What does Zweig advise?
options: Stock-picking isn’t for you: get an index fund
Start investing real money to improve your picks
Double your bets next year to catch up the gap
Switch to a more aggressive method of picking
questions.why: Only if you enjoyed the experiment and earned good returns should you build a basket of shares, and even then keep it to 10% of the portfolio.

questions.q: A dissolving company reports book value of R28.50 a share, much of it in cash. The share trades at R21.50. What gross profit would full realisation of book value give?
options: About 33%
About 25%
About 7%
About 50%
questions.why: (R28.50 − R21.50) ÷ R21.50 ≈ 33%. In Universal-Marion’s case, the share later fell as low as 13 after a first distribution, casting doubt on the outcome.

questions.q: Graham argues that a clever device like a conversion privilege cannot make a deal much better for both sides.
questions.why: The buyer usually gives up quality, yield or both. If the company raises money more cheaply, it gives away part of its shareholders’ future gains.

questions.q: Graham found that convertibles issued in the later stages of a bull market tend, as a group, to do well.
questions.why: They are bound to give unsatisfactory results, since a broad market fall makes the conversion privilege less attractive and often questions the issue’s safety too.

questions.q: In 1968–70, Graham’s sample of convertible preferreds fell about 29%, against about 10% for straight preferreds rated A or better.
questions.why: Ordinary shares in the sample fell 33% and listed warrants 65%. Of the 20 convertible preferreds, only one rose and 14 fell badly.

questions.q: The old Wall Street maxim Graham quotes is: “Always convert a convertible bond once it shows a profit.”
questions.why: The maxim is “Never convert a convertible bond.” Converting gives up the prior claim to interest and often turns an investor into a speculator at a poor time.

questions.q: Graham says the soundness of investing in convertibles can only be tested by how they perform in a falling market.
questions.why: In the long 1950–1968 bull market most shares rose, so most convertibles shared the gains. In declines, the record has been disappointing.

questions.q: Graham thinks warrants benefit the issuing company by guaranteeing it more capital when it needs it.
questions.why: The company usually can’t make holders exercise before expiry. If it needs equity, it must still offer shares to shareholders; the warrants only complicate matters.

questions.q: Graham’s simplest way to allow for warrants is to add their market value to the market value of the ordinary shares.
questions.why: That gives a “true” market price per share. The usual method, assuming the proceeds retire debt, ignores the premium warrants carry above exercise value.

questions.q: Over the years, buyers of AT&T’s convertible bonds did better than investors who simply bought AT&T shares.
questions.why: They fared well, but not quite as well as if they had bought the shares in the first place. AT&T proved the company sound, not convertibles.

questions.q: Zweig notes that convertibles’ returns move much more closely with shares than with government bonds.
questions.why: They are about 83% correlated with the S&P 500 and only about 30% with Treasury bonds: “stocks for chickens”.

questions.q: Zweig describes writing covered calls as a way to cushion losses without giving up any upside.
questions.why: It puts a floor under losses but a ceiling over gains. Since gains are unlimited and losses capped at 100%, he says it mostly enriches your broker.

questions.q: Graham calls stock-option warrants “a near fraud, an existing menace, and a potential disaster”.
questions.why: He says they create huge “values” out of thin air and should be banned, or strictly limited to a minor part of a company’s capital.

questions.q: What does Graham conclude the addition of a conversion privilege often reveals about an issue?
options: An absence of genuine investment quality
Exceptional strength in the company
That the shares are undervalued
That interest rates are about to fall
questions.why: Other things equal, a convertible beats a straight issue. In practice, other things are not equal: a really strong new issue rarely has a good conversion privilege.

questions.q: What is Graham’s “ideal combination” in a convertible, and where is it most likely found?
options: Strong security, an attractive share and a conversion price just above the market, more often in older issues
A high coupon and a long maturity, found mostly in new issues brought by the leading underwriters
Convertibility into a fast-growing share at any conversion price, found mainly in technology issues
Any convertible from a well-known company, since its name and size protect the bondholder from loss
questions.why: Older issues sometimes drift into a favourable position. New flotations rarely offer the combination.

questions.q: Experienced funds converted their profitable Eversharp debentures into shares and held them through a 90% fall. Why does Graham think they did it?
options: They were carried away by enthusiasm for the company and the shares’ “favourable market action”
The trust deed’s rules forced them to convert once the share price passed a set level
The shares paid a higher income than the interest on the debentures they gave up
They expected the fall and converted early so they could claim a tax loss when the shares dropped
questions.why: Wall Street has a few prudent principles, he says; the trouble is that they are always forgotten when most needed. Hence: “Do as I say, not as I do.”

questions.q: How do warrants take value away from ordinary shareholders?
options: They split off the shareholders’ right to subscribe for new shares and sell it as a separate certificate
They reduce the dividends the company may pay until the warrants have been exercised or expire
They give warrant holders voting control over the board until the warrants are finally exercised
They raise the company’s interest costs, because lenders charge more when warrants are outstanding
questions.why: People don’t realise the shares are worth less with warrants outstanding, so the package often sells for more than the shares alone.

questions.q: When does Graham NOT object to warrants?
options: When attached in moderate amounts to bond issues; a big warrant issue suggests a top-heavy structure
When they are perpetual, since holders then have unlimited time to exercise them at a profit
When the warrant issue is larger than the share issue, which shows confidence in the company
Never: he objects to every warrant, whether it is issued alone or attached to bonds or shares
questions.why: His attack is on the wanton creation of huge “paper-money” monstrosities. A company with a big warrant issue should be selling more ordinary shares instead.

questions.q: A convertible you own has risen 25% with the share. What dilemma does Graham describe?
options: Sell and risk the pain of selling too soon, or hold, effectively as a shareholder, and risk a collapse
Convert at once to lock in the gain, or keep the bond and give up the income it pays you
Buy more of the bonds to average up, or sell the shares short to protect the profit you have made
None: a rising convertible carries no risk, since the bond’s face value protects the holder
questions.why: Hold for more and your bond moves with the share. A stern rule of selling at 25–30% caps gains, while issues that never rise can still collapse.

questions.q: In 1970, why might owners of Studebaker-Worthington ordinary shares have switched into its convertible preferred?
options: The preferred paid far more income, ranked ahead of the shares and couldn’t sell below what it converted into
The preferred was much cheaper than the ordinary shares, so the switch produced an immediate profit
The ordinary shares were about to be cancelled as part of a merger, leaving only the preferred listed
Preferred dividends were tax-free for individuals, while dividends on the ordinary shares were taxed
questions.why: The small price gap would be recovered from the dividend difference in under a year, and the switch gave a senior position at no real cost.

questions.q: What does Zweig suggest for an individual who wants convertibles?
options: A low-cost convertible fund, with expenses below 1% a year
Buying small lots of individual convertibles
Structured products that promise a floor under losses
Convertibles issued near the end of a bull market
questions.why: Small lots are expensive to trade, and diversifying needs well over $100,000. Complex variants with acronym names are generally more trouble than they’re worth.

questions.q: A R1,000 bond is convertible into shares at R25 each. The share rises to R30. What is the bond’s conversion value?
options: R1,200: 40 shares × R30
R1,000: its face value
R750: 25 shares × R30
R1,250: the market price
questions.why: R1,000 ÷ R25 = 40 shares, and 40 × R30 = R1,200, or 120. Graham’s example has the bond selling at 125, a 25% profit.

questions.q: A convertible bond converts into 24.24 shares, now R5.66 each, and trades at R881.30. What is its conversion premium?
options: About 542%
About 84%
About 16%
About 24%
questions.why: Conversion value is 24.24 × R5.66 ≈ R137.20, and (R881.30 − R137.20) ÷ R137.20 ≈ 542%. That was DoubleClick at the end of 2002.

questions.q: For that same bond (24.24 shares per bond, bond price R881.30), roughly what share price would make converting worth as much as the bond?
options: About R36
About R6
About R24
About R88
questions.why: R881.30 ÷ 24.24 ≈ R36.36, more than six times the share’s R5.66. Zweig says such a rise borders on the miraculous.

questions.q: You pay about R744 above a convertible’s conversion value, and it pays R47.50 interest a year. Roughly how many years of interest does it take to earn back the premium?
options: About 16 years
About 5 years
About 10 years
About 1.6 years
questions.why: R744 ÷ R47.50 ≈ 15.7 years. Zweig calls this the payback period: the cash yield scarcely seems adequate.

questions.q: A R1,000 debenture converts into 37.5 shares (after a 3-for-2 split). The shares fall to R7.375. Roughly what is its conversion value?
options: About R277, or about 27% of face value
About R737, or about 74% of face value
About R1,000, its full face value
About R184, or about 18% of face value
questions.why: 37.5 × R7.375 ≈ R277. Eversharp’s holders who converted near the top turned a 100%-plus profit into a loss of about three-quarters.

questions.q: A share trades at R57. A convertible preferred trades at R87.50 and converts into 1½ shares. The preferred pays R5 a year; each share pays R1.20. How long does the preferred’s extra income take to cover its higher price?
options: Under a year: R2 extra cost against R3.20 extra income
About 3 years: R9.50 extra cost against R3.20 a year
About 10 years: R32 extra cost against R3.20 a year
Never: the preferred pays less income than the shares
questions.why: 1½ shares cost R85.50, so the preferred costs R2 more. Its R5 dividend beats 1½ × R1.20 = R1.80 by R3.20 a year, and it ranks ahead.

questions.q: A share trades at R24.50. Its warrants have a total market value of R94m, and there are 5 million shares. EPS is R2.33. What is the warrant-adjusted P/E, by Graham’s method?
options: About 18.6
About 10.5
About 15.3
About 40
questions.why: R94m ÷ 5m = R18.80 a share, so the true price is R43.30, and R43.30 ÷ R2.33 ≈ 18.6. That was National General in 1971.

questions.q: You buy 100 shares at R95 and write a call at R100 for a R10 premium. The share jumps to R130 and is called away. What is your total gain, and what would it have been without the call?
options: R1,500, against R3,500
R3,500, against R1,500
R1,000, against R3,500
R3,500 either way
questions.why: (R100 − R95 + R10) × 100 = R1,500. Holding alone would give (R130 − R95) × 100 = R3,500. The premium buys a ceiling on your gains.

questions.q: Same covered call: bought at R95, R10 premium received. This time the share falls to R60. What is your loss per share?
options: Nothing: the call protects you
questions.why: (R60 − R95) + R10 = −R25. The premium cushions only R10 of a R35 fall: limited protection for a capped upside.

questions.q: Graham says the simplest rules of security analysis would have revealed Penn Central’s fundamental weakness by 1968 at the latest.
questions.why: That was when its shares stood at their post-1929 record. No competent adviser should have held its bonds or shares after that.

questions.q: Graham’s minimum interest cover for railroad bonds is 2 times earnings before tax, averaged over seven years.
questions.why: It is 5 times before income tax (2.9 times after). Penn Central covered its interest less than 2 times before tax.

questions.q: Penn Central had paid almost no income tax for 11 years, which Graham says should have raised questions about its reported earnings.
questions.why: Any analyst worth his salt would wonder how “real” profits were if no tax was ever paid on them.

questions.q: Graham says Penn Central bondholders had no safer alternative without giving up price or income.
questions.why: In 1968–69 they could have swapped at about even prices into far better-covered utility bonds with similar coupons. It would have been a lifesaver.

questions.q: Ling-Temco-Vought’s losses in 1969 and 1970 far exceeded all the profits it had made since it was formed.
questions.why: Its debt had reached $1,865 million, its share fell from 169½ to 7⅛, and its largest bond issue traded at one point at 15 cents on the dollar.

questions.q: In the LTV story, Graham puts the main question mark over the regulators rather than the lenders.
questions.why: His primary question is how commercial banks could be persuaded to lend so much, nearly $400 million more in two years, when the ratios already failed conservative standards.

questions.q: NVF took over Sharon Steel, a company about seven times its own size.
questions.why: Sharon had $219 million of sales against NVF’s $31 million. Graham calls it the most extreme of 1969’s takeovers in its financial disproportions.

questions.q: AAA Enterprises’ share price fell sharply soon after its 1969 public offering, as buyers lost interest.
questions.why: It promptly doubled from 13 to 28, valuing the company at $84 million against a book value of about $4.2 million.

questions.q: Graham suggests reputable houses of 1914 would have shunned ventures like AAA Enterprises, and that ethical standards have since fallen.
questions.why: He asks whether such houses should be honour-bound to avoid enterprises, nine out of ten of which may be foredoomed, and whether the SEC needs wider powers.

questions.q: AOL’s holders were to get 55% of AOL–Time Warner, though Time Warner was about five times bigger than AOL.
questions.why: AOL’s shares sold at 164 times earnings. By the end of 2002 shareholders had lost roughly 80% since the deal was announced.

questions.q: eToys was modestly profitable in the 20 months before its 1999 public offering, though its sales were small.
questions.why: It lost $30.8 million on sales of $30.6 million, spending about $2 to sell every dollar of toys. It was still valued above Toys “R” Us.

questions.q: Which “extreme” does Graham use NVF Corp. to illustrate?
options: A small company absorbing one seven times its size, with huge debt and startling accounting devices
Neglect of the warning signs at a tottering giant whose history made investors feel safe
A hot new issue built on franchising, sold to a public that ignored the company’s tiny earnings
Unsound empire building, helped along by generous bank lending and a string of rapid takeovers
questions.why: Penn Central, LTV and AAA Enterprises illustrate the other three extremes.

questions.q: Penn Central reported 1966 earnings of $6.80 a share, while a $12-a-share charge for merger “costs and losses” was to be taken later. What is Graham’s point?
options: Profits shown in one place and losses in another can fool shareholders: always check the special charges
Merger costs never matter to shareholders, since they are spread over the life of the merged company
The $12 charge was a sign of strength, showing the railroad could afford to clean up its accounts
Railroads always report conservatively, so their headline earnings understate what they truly earn
questions.why: “O wondrous fairyland of Wall Street,” he writes. Zweig links it to the “pro forma” accounting of the late 1990s.

questions.q: In 1961, LTV threw about $13 million of charges and reserves into one bad year, more than its previous three years’ profits combined. What did that achieve?
options: It cleared the way for “record earnings” the following year
It reduced the company’s debt by the amount of the charges
It raised the share price immediately, as investors cheered
It allowed the company to increase its dividend that year
questions.why: Zweig calls this “big bath” or “kitchen sink” accounting: an easy show of growth next year, not real business health.

questions.q: NVF’s new 5% bonds never traded above 42 cents on the dollar during their first year. What did that signal?
options: Grave doubt about the bonds’ safety and the company’s future
That the bonds were a bargain with very little risk attached
That interest rates had fallen sharply during the year
That the takeover had made NVF a much stronger company
questions.why: Management even exploited the low bond price to save about $1 million a year in tax. Later NVF spent borrowed money buying back warrants.

questions.q: At the end of 1970 the Stock Guide showed NVF at a P/E of only 2, the lowest of some 4,500 issues. Why was this misleading?
options: It ignored heavy dilution and a bad last quarter: full-year EPS was $2.03, or $1.80 diluted, not the $5.38 used
The share price in the Guide was out of date, and the shares had already risen more than fivefold
NVF had no debt, so its earnings were far more reliable than those of the other 4,500 issues
The Guide double-counted NVF’s dividends and earnings, which made the shares look far cheaper than they were
questions.why: “Important if true,” as the old saying went. Shares and warrants together were worth about $14 million against $135 million of bonds.

questions.q: AAA Enterprises’ offering lifted its equity per share from 59 cents to $1.35. Why does Graham call this a “bootstrap operation”?
options: The rise came from the buying public’s own money, paid at about ten times book value
The company earned the increase from its operations during the year of the offering
The founder put in his own capital to lift the equity before the shares were sold
The underwriters guaranteed the new value, so the public bought at no real risk
questions.why: Investors paid heavily in advance for hoped-for plans. Before 1968 the company’s best earnings had been 7 cents a share.

questions.q: What is Graham’s judgment on the speculative public, after the AAA Enterprises story?
options: It is incorrigible: it can’t count beyond 3 and will buy anything at any price if there seems to be “action”
It learns quickly from its losses, so the next hot issue will find far fewer buyers than the last
It is protected well enough by the prospectus rules, which disclose every risk a buyer faces
It avoids fashionable industries after a crash, which is why franchising issues fell out of favour
questions.why: AAA still closed 1969 at 8⅛ bid, valuing it at over $25 million, though it had lost nearly all its capital.

questions.q: Tyco booked “nonrecurring” merger and restructuring charges in four of five years. What question does Zweig say an investor should ask?
options: If the business is buying companies, aren’t these simply normal, recurring costs of doing business?
How soon will the charges make the shares cheap enough to buy at a discount to the market?
Should the charges be added back to earnings, since they won’t happen again once deals stop?
Why didn’t Tyco buy even more companies, given that each new deal added to its reported earnings?
questions.why: Tyco spent an average of about $750 million a year cleaning up after its acquisitions. In fiscal 2002 it lost $9.4 billion.

questions.q: Which of these was NOT one of the warning signs in Lucent’s mid-2000 report?
options: A sharp cut in its dividend
$4.2 billion of goodwill paid for a company with no customers and no revenue
Loans to customers that had doubled in a year
Software development costs treated as an asset
questions.why: Lucent later lost $16.2 billion and $11.9 billion in two years, and its share fell from about $51 to $1.26.

questions.q: A railway earns R191m before interest and tax and pays R100m in interest, but pays almost no tax. How does it compare with Graham’s standard?
options: Cover of 1.91 times, far below the 5 times required before tax
Cover of 1.91 times, which meets the 2.9-times after-tax test
Cover of 5 times on average, so it passes Graham’s standard
Cover of 0.5 times, so it is already in default on its interest
questions.why: R191m ÷ R100m = 1.91. With no tax being paid, the before-tax test of 5 times is the one that applies, as with Penn Central.

questions.q: In 1969 you hold R10,000 face value of railway bonds at 70, and could swap into a much better-covered utility bond at the same price and coupon. A year later the railway bonds are at 18½ and the utility bonds at 66½. What did not swapping cost you?
options: About R4,800: R1,850 against R6,650
About R480: R6,170 against R6,650
Nothing: both bonds fell in the panic
About R1,850: the value left in the railway bonds
questions.why: R10,000 × 0.185 = R1,850 and R10,000 × 0.665 = R6,650. Graham calls the Penn Central swap clearly called for, and a lifesaver.

questions.q: A share reaches R169.50 when its net tangible assets are R7.66 a share. What multiple of tangible assets is that?
options: About 22 times
About 7.7 times
About 2.2 times
About 169 times
questions.why: R169.50 ÷ R7.66 ≈ 22. That was LTV in 1967; three years later its share was 7⅛.

questions.q: A company’s reported equity is R40.2m. It includes a R58.6m “deferred debt expense” asset, and excludes a R20.7m “excess of equity over cost” item. Roughly what is its realistic tangible equity?
options: About R2.2m
About R40.2m
About R119.5m
About R60.9m
questions.why: R40.2m − R58.6m + R20.7m ≈ R2.3m. That was NVF after the Sharon deal: about $3 a share, down from $23.71.

questions.q: A new issue’s market value soars to R84m. Its book value is R4.2m and its best-ever annual earnings were R0.69m. Roughly what multiples is the market paying?
options: About 20 times book and over 100 times earnings
About 2 times book and 12 times earnings
About 4 times book and 20 times earnings
About 84 times book and 4 times earnings
questions.why: R84m ÷ R4.2m = 20, and R84m ÷ R0.69m ≈ 122. AAA Enterprises sold at about 115 times its largest earnings per share.

questions.q: A company pays R4.8bn for a start-up with no revenue, of which R4.2bn is goodwill. What share of the price is goodwill?
options: About 87.5%
About 12.5%
About 50%
questions.why: R4.2bn ÷ R4.8bn = 87.5%. Zweig suggests “hope chest” might describe Lucent’s Chromatis goodwill better; the unit was shut down within a year.

questions.q: A company has 102 million shares and has reserved another 40.6 million for management. If it later earns R143m, what are EPS before and after the reserved shares are issued?
options: About R1.40 before, about R1.00 after: dilution of nearly a third
About R1.40 either way, since reserved shares aren’t counted
About R1.00 before, about R1.40 after: the reserve adds value
About R3.52 either way, since dilution only affects the price
questions.why: R143m ÷ 102m ≈ R1.40, and R143m ÷ 142.6m ≈ R1.00. That was eToys’ reserve for its managers.

questions.q: A company sold R30.6m of goods and made a net loss of R30.8m. Roughly how much did it spend for each R1 of sales?
options: About R2
About R1
About R0.50
About R30
questions.why: Costs ≈ R30.6m + R30.8m = R61.4m, and R61.4m ÷ R30.6m ≈ R2. eToys was still valued at $7.8 billion on its first day.

questions.q: Real Estate Investment Trust had paid dividends continuously since 1889.
questions.why: It was a staid New England trust that kept to prudent investments, moderate growth and manageable debt.

questions.q: In 1968, Wall Street paid most attention to the steady Trust and little to the fast-expanding Realty Equities.
questions.why: The reverse: Realty Equities shot from 10 to 37¾ on heavy volume, while the Trust rose sedately. Equities’ auditors later refused to certify its accounts.

questions.q: Realty Equities’ March 1969 balance sheet showed asset value of $3.41 a share, less than a tenth of its high price that year.
questions.why: The Trust’s book value was $20.85. A year later Equities reported a loss that virtually wiped out its slim equity.

questions.q: Graham states firmly that Air Reduction was a better buy than Air Products at their 1969 prices.
questions.why: He doubts it can be answered definitively. Low-multiplier companies as a group may do better, so Air Reduction gets the preference, but only as part of a diversified operation.

questions.q: Graham judged both American Home Products and American Hospital Supply too “rich” for a conservative investor at their 1969 prices.
questions.why: Their combined price reflected almost $5 billion of goodwill: too much promise and not enough actual performance.

questions.q: At the end of 1969, the market valued H&R Block at only about 10 times its tangible assets.
questions.why: It was nearly 30 times, almost unheard of in serious valuations. IBM then sold at about 9 times book and Xerox at 11.

questions.q: International Flavors & Fragrances was worth more on the market than International Harvester, though Harvester had 27 times its sales.
questions.why: Flavors earned 14.3% on sales and 19.7% on capital; Harvester, 2.6% and 5.5%. Profitability and growth were the “two magic words”.

questions.q: International Flavors & Fragrances built its success mainly through acquisitions and complex financing.
questions.why: Its success came entirely from developing its central business, with no wheeling and dealing. It “stuck to its extremely profitable knitting”.

questions.q: Graham said McGraw-Hill’s price at the end of 1968 illustrated “the triumph of hope over experience”.
questions.why: It sold at 35 times earnings and over eight times tangible assets after two years of falling profits. By May 1970 it had dropped to 10.

questions.q: National General’s own “full dilution” calculation sharply reduced its reported 1968 earnings per share.
questions.why: It had virtually no effect: $1.51 before and after. Graham calls the method illogical; adding the warrants’ market value more than doubles the true price.

questions.q: Zweig writes that there is no such thing as a good stock, only good stock prices, which come and go.
questions.why: At some point almost every share is a bargain, and at another it is expensive. The cheap may become dear, and the dear cheap.

questions.q: In each of 13 years, McGraw-Hill’s share price rose or fell by a ratio of at least three to two from one year to the next.
questions.why: Investors must be prepared for adverse moves like these, which affected most of the companies in this chapter in 1961–62 and 1969–70.

questions.q: American Home Products had a very low book value relative to its price. What “basic ambiguity” does Graham see in this?
options: It shows a high return on capital, a strength, but leaves the buyer exposed to any setback in earnings
It proves the shares are cheap, since a low book value means the assets are hidden in the accounts
It means the company is close to insolvency, since its liabilities nearly equal its assets
It has no bearing on risk, since only earnings and dividends matter to a buyer of the shares
questions.why: With little asset backing, almost all the price depends on earnings continuing. The same caution applied to Hospital at over four times book.

questions.q: An experienced analyst would grant H&R Block excellent momentum. What would his chief concern be?
options: Whether the $300 million valuation already priced in, or more than priced in, all one could expect
Whether its accounts were reliable, since its growth seemed too fast to be explained by its business
Whether it would keep paying dividends, since a young company often needs its cash for expansion
Whether it had taken on too much debt, since tax-preparation offices are costly to open
questions.why: Blue Bell, by contrast, was a fine company quite conservatively priced, and it proved the better buy as of the end of 1969.

questions.q: H&R Block still rose about 35% from its apparently inflated 1969 price. What lesson does Graham draw?
options: Be very wary of selling good companies short, however high the price seems
Overvalued shares keep rising for years, so buy them whatever the price
High P/E ratios are a sign of safety, because the market trusts the company
Short selling is the best way to profit once a share looks overvalued
questions.why: Zweig adds that an overvalued share can stay overvalued for a surprisingly long time, making short-selling too risky for mere mortals.

questions.q: What question does International Harvester’s record raise for Graham?
options: Why huge companies earned so little even in good years, and what use vast sales are without an adequate return
Why it took on so much debt to pay for acquisitions in industries it didn’t understand or know how to run
Why it had stopped paying dividends, even though its sales were among the largest in the country
Why its accounting was so complex that even trained analysts couldn’t work out its true earnings
questions.why: He insists that shareholders, not only management, should be conscious of the problem. Even at a discount, its showing was too mediocre to be really attractive.

questions.q: After studying these pairs, how does Graham say an analyst’s work is most dependable and rewarding?
options: Seeking the exceptional, minority cases where he can confidently judge the price to be well below value
Choosing the shares that are likely to have the best market action over the next twelve months
Predicting which industries will grow fastest, and then choosing the leading company in each of them
Following the most popular shares of the day, since the crowd’s favourites tend to keep rising
questions.why: He is frankly sceptical that picking the best future performers can be done with satisfactory results.

questions.q: Zweig borrows Ambrose Bierce’s word “incompossible”. What two things does he say cannot coexist?
options: Being a giant company and deserving a giant P/E ratio
Paying high dividends and achieving high growth
Having low debt and earning high returns on capital
Rising sales and falling profits in the same year
questions.why: Once a company is huge, growth must slow. No company as big as Cisco had grown fast enough to justify a P/E above 60, let alone over 200.

questions.q: Ball and Stryker both fell sharply in July 2002 as the market plunged, despite good news. What does Zweig conclude?
options: Panics can create great prices for good companies and good prices for great companies
Ball was a steal at that price, while buying Stryker after the fall was a mistake
Good news no longer affects share prices once the whole market is falling
Investors should sell in falling markets and buy back once the panic is over
questions.why: Both recovered strongly by year-end. Value and growth shares alike go on sale from time to time.

questions.q: Why did Yahoo!’s share jump 63.6% in five trading days in December 1999?
options: Its inclusion in the S&P 500 forced index funds to buy, while about 90% of its shares were locked up
It reported a sudden surge in profits, which analysts had not expected until the following year
It announced its first large dividend, which drew income investors to the share for the first time
It was taken over at a large premium by a bigger media company looking to expand online
questions.why: Thousands bought only because others would have to buy, and price was no object. By the end of 2002 it had lost 92.4%.

questions.q: Complete Graham’s saying, as quoted by Zweig: in the short run the market is a voting machine, but in the long run it is…
options: a weighing machine
a slot machine
a counting machine
a printing machine
questions.why: Yahoo! won the short-term popularity contest, but once the market started weighing earnings, Yum! came out ahead.

questions.q: National Presto met all Graham’s tests in 1968. What caution did he still attach to its growth figures?
options: They were suspiciously good, boosted by war work, so profits might fall in peacetime
They had been fabricated, since the auditors had resigned shortly before the results
They came entirely from acquisitions, so the existing business had not grown at all
They depended on a single customer, whose bankruptcy would wipe out most of the profit
questions.why: Even so, by 1970 it sold at under four times earnings and below its net current assets: ten such issues would make a satisfactory group.

questions.q: A company’s ordinary shares are worth R192m and its warrants R221m; it has 4.33m shares and EPS of R1.42. What are the warrant-adjusted price and P/E, roughly?
options: About R95 a share and about 67 times earnings
About R44 a share and about 31 times earnings
About R51 a share and about 36 times earnings
About R192 a share and about 135 times earnings
questions.why: (R192m + R221m) ÷ 4.33m ≈ R95, and R95 ÷ R1.42 ≈ 67. Graham found National General at an “inherently absurd” 69 times.

questions.q: Each 3Com share was to receive 1.525 Palm shares. Palm closed at R95.06 and 3Com at R81.81. What did this imply for 3Com’s other businesses?
options: About minus R63 a share: the Palm stake alone was worth about R145
About R81.81 a share: the market price is the best estimate
About R13 a share: the difference between the two share prices
About R177 a share: the 3Com price plus the Palm share price
questions.why: 1.525 × R95.06 ≈ R144.97, and R81.81 − R144.97 ≈ −R63.16. Rarely has a share been priced more stupidly; but Palm, at 1,350 times earnings, was the real folly.

questions.q: A restaurant group is worth R5.9bn, with R8bn of revenue and R633m of net income. Roughly what are its price-to-earnings and price-to-sales ratios?
options: About 9 times earnings and 0.74 times sales
About 13 times earnings and 1.4 times sales
About 63 times earnings and 8 times sales
About 0.1 times earnings and 1.4 times sales
questions.why: R5.9bn ÷ R633m ≈ 9.3, and R5.9bn ÷ R8bn ≈ 0.74. That was Yum! at the end of 1999; it rose 25% over the next three years.

questions.q: A company is worth R114bn, with R433m of revenue and R34.9m of net income. Roughly what are its price-to-sales and P/E ratios?
options: About 263 times sales and about 3,266 times earnings
About 26 times sales and about 326 times earnings
About 2.6 times sales and about 33 times earnings
About 433 times sales and about 114 times earnings
questions.why: R114bn ÷ R0.433bn ≈ 263, and R114bn ÷ R0.0349bn ≈ 3,266. That was Yahoo! at the end of 1999.

questions.q: A share trades at R24.75 and its book value is R41.70 a share. At what discount to net worth is it selling?
options: About 41%
About 59%
About 17%
It trades at a premium of about 68%
questions.why: R24.75 ÷ R41.70 ≈ 0.59, a 41% discount. That was International Harvester at the end of 1969, still too mediocre to be really attractive.

questions.q: A young company lost R63m on R34m of revenue. If revenue grows to R140m and the loss per rand of sales stays the same, roughly what would it lose?
options: About R260m
About R63m
About R140m
It would break even
questions.why: It loses about R1.85 per rand of sales, and R140m × 1.85 ≈ R260m. Zweig’s point on Commerce One: faster growth just meant bigger losses.

questions.q: Using Graham’s formula (multiplier = 8.5 + 2 × growth), what annual growth rate would a P/E of 219 imply?
options: About 105% a year
About 22% a year
About 50% a year
About 219% a year
questions.why: 219 = 8.5 + 2g gives g ≈ 105% a year for seven to ten years: impossible for a giant like Cisco in 2000.

questions.q: A share trades at R17.75, earns R1.91 and pays a dividend of R1.50. What are its P/E and dividend yield?
options: About 9.3 times and about 8.5%
About 11.8 times and about 5.5%
About 9.3 times and about 1.5%
About 1.2 times and about 10.8%
questions.why: R17.75 ÷ R1.91 ≈ 9.3, and R1.50 ÷ R17.75 ≈ 8.5%. That was Whiting, a sound secondary issue, against a conglomerate worth four times as much.

questions.q: A trust earned R2.696m before interest and paid R0.59m of interest. A rival earned R11.18m before interest and paid R6.68m. Roughly what are their interest covers?
options: About 4.6 times against about 1.7 times
About 1.7 times against about 4.6 times
About 2.7 times against about 11 times
About the same, at 4.6 times
questions.why: R2.696m ÷ R0.59m ≈ 4.6 and R11.18m ÷ R6.68m ≈ 1.7. The bigger, faster-growing Realty Equities was far more fragile.

questions.q: A packaging company is worth R1.9bn, with trailing earnings of R152m and book value of R1.1bn. Roughly what are its P/E and price-to-book?
options: About 12.5 times earnings and 1.7 times book
About 7 times earnings and 0.6 times book
About 30 times earnings and 16 times book
About 1.25 times earnings and 17 times book
questions.why: R1.9bn ÷ R152m = 12.5, and R1.9bn ÷ R1.1bn ≈ 1.7. That was Ball after the July 2002 slump; Stryker sold at 30 times earnings and nearly 16 times book.

questions.q: Graham says shareholders may question management when results are poor, worse than at similar companies, and keep the share price down.
questions.why: Those are his three tests. He also asks shareholders to be generous to managements that are demonstrably doing a good job.

questions.q: Graham says public shareholders, voting together, have often succeeded in replacing poor managements.
questions.why: In 36 years practically nothing was accomplished that way. Poor managements change when an individual or compact group takes control, usually through a takeover.

questions.q: In earlier times, companies typically paid out 60% to 75% of their earnings as dividends.
questions.why: Back then it was usually the weak company that was forced to hold on to its profits, which hurt its share price. Zweig notes payout ratios fell to 35–40% by the late 1990s.

questions.q: Texas Instruments’ share rose from 5 to 256 between 1953 and 1960 while paying generous dividends.
questions.why: It paid no dividend at all. For growth favourites, the dividend, or its absence, seemed to have virtually no effect on the price.

questions.q: Shareholders, Graham says, should demand a payout of about two-thirds of earnings, or proof that reinvestment has raised per-share earnings.
questions.why: A recognised growth company can usually show this. Elsewhere a low payout often keeps the price below fair value, and shareholders have every right to complain.

questions.q: Graham supports mediocre companies holding back dividends so that their existing management can expand the business.
questions.why: He calls it illogical on its face. There is no reason to expect owners to benefit from expansion by a business with mediocre results and the same management.

questions.q: The New York Stock Exchange used 25% as the practical dividing line between stock dividends and stock splits.
questions.why: Distributions of 25% or more did not need their market value transferred from earned surplus to capital.

questions.q: Graham agrees with academic writers that periodic stock dividends are just meaningless pieces of paper.
questions.why: He calls that view completely doctrinaire. The new certificates are a convenient way to cash in reinvested profits, and the cash dividend rate is often kept on the larger number of shares.

questions.q: Only 3.7% of US companies that listed in 1999 paid a dividend, against an average of 72.1% of new issues in the 1960s.
questions.why: Zweig calls the idea that managers know best what to do with shareholders’ cash “Daddy Knows Best”, and “nothing but bunk”.

questions.q: Zweig argues that share buybacks always help shareholders, because they raise the earnings per share that remain.
questions.why: In theory they can, especially when shares are cheap. In practice, many companies bought back expensive shares mainly to offset the dilution from executives’ options.

questions.q: Zweig suggests voting against any option plan that would hand managers more than 3% of the company’s shares.
questions.why: He would also veto grants not tied to a fair, lasting measure of superior results, such as beating the industry average over at least five years.

questions.q: What does Graham say rescued the cause of shareholders against poor managements?
options: Takeover bids: poor management brings low prices, which attract companies and groups seeking control
Annual meetings, where shareholders regularly voted out managers who had failed to perform
New government regulation, which forced boards to report on management performance each year
Stock exchange listing rules, which required a majority of independent directors on every board
questions.why: The bid price has usually been near the value under competent management. Boards now know that poor results may make them a target.

questions.q: In the 1949 edition, which two basic questions did Graham say shareholders should ask?
options: Is the management reasonably efficient? Are outside shareholders’ interests receiving proper recognition?
Will the share price rise over the next year? Will the dividend be raised at the next meeting?
Is the company growing faster than its rivals? Is its industry growing faster than the economy?
Is the chief executive well known in the business press? Is the company included in the main index?
questions.why: Judge efficiency by comparing profitability, size and competitiveness with similar firms in the industry.

questions.q: How does Graham describe the market’s treatment of dividends for “income issues” compared with recognised rapid-growth shares?
options: For income issues the dividend still largely sets the price; for growth shares it is more or less ignored
Dividends matter equally for both, since every share’s price is the present value of its dividends
Dividends matter only for growth shares, since investors pay up for companies that raise them fast
Dividends matter for neither, since the market prices all shares on their reported earnings alone
questions.why: Many companies sit in between, and the market’s view of them can change radically from year to year.

questions.q: What does Graham call a “proper” stock dividend?
options: A small issue (usually 5% or less) representing earnings reinvested over about the past two years
Any issue of two or three new shares for each one held, to bring the price into a popular range
A dividend paid in shares of another company that the business holds as an investment
An issue of 25% or more of the shares in issue, made to lower the price of each share
questions.why: A split restates the share structure to lower the price per share. A proper stock dividend capitalises recent reinvested earnings.

questions.q: What did Enron’s 1999 proxy statement disclose that should have alarmed a careful reader?
options: Its finance director ran partnerships that bought assets from Enron, sometimes with Enron’s money, and shared their profits
That its auditors had resigned during the year and been replaced by a smaller firm without any public explanation
That it had stopped paying dividends to ordinary shareholders while keeping its directors’ bonuses unchanged
That its revenues were falling in every division, which the annual report had described as a year of steady growth
questions.why: His duty was to get the best price for Enron; his personal interest was the opposite. Zweig’s lesson: read the proxy, before and after you buy.

questions.q: Graham distinguished efficient operations from efficient finance. What did he say managements tend to do with capital?
options: Keep as much of the owners’ capital as shareholders allow, running the business with more than it needs
Return all surplus cash promptly to shareholders, since idle cash lowers the company’s return on capital
Borrow as much as the banks will lend, so that the owners’ money stays free for dividends
Invest the surplus only in government bonds, so that the owners’ capital is never put at risk
questions.why: Managers want to minimise their own financial problems. Zweig points to Microsoft’s cash pile of over $38 billion, growing by more than $2 million an hour.

questions.q: What did Robert Arnott and Clifford Asness find about dividends and later earnings growth?
options: When dividends were high, earnings growth over the next decade was higher, by about 3.9 points a year
Higher dividends led to lower earnings growth, because less money was kept for reinvestment
Dividends had no link at all with later earnings growth once company size was taken into account
Only the companies that paid no dividend at all managed to grow their earnings over the decade
questions.why: Other research found that companies raising their dividend showed higher profitability for at least four years afterwards.

questions.q: Why might a chief executive paid mainly in options prefer buybacks to dividends?
options: Options gain value when the share price is more volatile, and dividends dampen volatility
Dividends can’t legally be paid to executives who hold options on the company’s shares
Buybacks are always cheaper for the company than dividends, so they leave more for growth
