Dividends must be approved by the regulators each year, while buybacks need no approval
questions.why: Companies also get a tax deduction when options are exercised. The outside shareholders’ interest can be lost in the arrangement.

questions.q: What did Graham propose that independent directors should do?
options: Report to shareholders each year on whether the business is earning what proper management should, and if not, why
Approve all of management’s proposals unanimously, so that shareholders always see a united and confident board
Set a share price target for management each year and replace the managers who miss it
Manage the company’s surplus cash and investment portfolio, so that executives can focus on operations
questions.why: Zweig imagines them also justifying dividend and buyback policy, and explaining how they decided management was not overpaid.

questions.q: A mature, slow-growing company earns R6.00 a share and pays a R1.50 dividend. What is its payout ratio, and what might Graham expect shareholders to ask?
options: 25%: well below a normal two-thirds, so they should ask for proof that retained profits raise earnings
25%: ideal for a mature company, since retained profits always add to the value of the business
75%: too high for a mature company, which should keep most of its profits to fund future growth
400%: unsustainable, since the company is paying out four times what it earns in each year
questions.why: R1.50 ÷ R6.00 = 25%. A normal payout on R6.00 would be about R4.00. Without proof that reinvestment pays, shareholders have every right to complain.

questions.q: You own 100 shares at R50, paying R2 each a year. The company pays a 5% stock dividend and keeps the R2 rate on the new shares. What happens?
options: You hold 105 shares, still worth about R5,000, and your income rises from R200 to R210
You hold 105 shares now worth R5,250, and your income stays at R200 a year
You still hold 100 shares, but they are now worth R5,250 because of the dividend
Nothing changes at all: you hold the same shares, worth the same, with the same income
questions.why: The stock dividend changes only the form of your holding, but keeping the cash rate on 105 shares is easier than a 5% rise in the rate on 100.

questions.q: A utility pays you a R10,000 cash dividend, taxed at 20%, then asks you to subscribe R10,000 for new shares through rights. Compared with simply receiving R10,000 of new shares as a stock dividend, where do you end up?
options: With the same shares, but R2,000 poorer because of the tax
With the same shares, and R2,000 richer from the cash dividend
In exactly the same position, since the cash simply came back
With fewer shares than before, but more cash left in hand
questions.why: You pay tax on money the company immediately takes back. Graham called this second tax completely inequitable.

questions.q: A company issues 100 million shares to insiders at an average of R3.53, then buys back 100 million shares at R18.26. What is the cost to outside shareholders, roughly?
options: About R1.47bn: it sold low and bought high
About R353m: the money raised from insiders
About R1.83bn: the full cost of the buyback
Nothing: the number of shares is unchanged
questions.why: (R18.26 − R3.53) × 100m ≈ R1.47bn. The share count is the same, but cash has gone out of the company. That was Oracle’s pattern in 1999–2000.

questions.q: A company earns R100m on 50 million shares and buys back 5 million. If profit is unchanged, what happens to EPS?
options: It rises from R2.00 to about R2.22, about 11%
It stays at R2.00, since profit is unchanged
It rises from R2.00 to R2.50, a 25% increase
It falls from R2.00 to about R1.82, about 9%
questions.why: R100m ÷ 45m ≈ R2.22. That is the theory: buybacks help when shares are cheap. Zweig’s warning is about what they cost when shares are dear.

questions.q: A company with 400 million shares proposes an option plan of 20 million shares for executives, with no performance hurdle. How should an intelligent owner vote?
options: Against: 5% of the shares is above Zweig’s 3% limit, and the grants aren’t tied to superior results
For: 5% of the shares is a modest price to pay for keeping talented executives motivated
For, provided the share price has been rising, which shows that the executives deserve it
Abstain: shareholders have no real say over pay, which the board’s committee decides alone
questions.why: 20m ÷ 400m = 5%. Grants should depend on a lasting measure of superior results, such as beating the industry for at least five years.

questions.q: From 1953 to 1960 a share rose from 5 to 256 while EPS grew from R0.43 to R3.91. Roughly how did its P/E change?
options: From about 12 to about 65 times
It stayed at about 12 times
From about 65 to about 12 times
From about 5 to about 9 times
questions.why: 5 ÷ 0.43 ≈ 11.6 and 256 ÷ 3.91 ≈ 65. The price rose about 51-fold on 9-fold earnings growth. Texas Instruments then fell to 49 by 1962 as earnings dropped.

questions.q: Asked to distil the secret of sound investment into three words, Graham chose “margin of safety”.
questions.why: He calls it the thread running through all his earlier discussion of investment policy, sometimes explicitly and sometimes less directly.

questions.q: Graham says the main function of the margin of safety is to make an accurate forecast of the future possible.
questions.why: It renders an accurate estimate of the future unnecessary. If the margin is large, it is enough to assume earnings won’t fall far below the past.

questions.q: Graham says the chief losses to investors come from buying low-quality securities when business conditions are favourable.
questions.why: Buyers treat current good earnings as earning power and assume prosperity means safety. Fair-weather investments at fair-weather prices fall when the horizon clouds.

questions.q: Graham says growth shares can never offer a margin of safety, because they depend on future earnings.
questions.why: They can, if the future is projected conservatively and shows a satisfactory margin against the price. The danger is that the market usually prices them too high for that.

questions.q: Graham’s rule is that any estimate differing from past performance must err at least slightly on the side of understatement.
questions.why: He calls it a basic rule of prudent investment. The margin of safety is always dependent on the price paid.

questions.q: A margin of safety guarantees that each individual holding in a portfolio will not lose money.
questions.why: It only gives a better chance of profit than loss. That is why it goes hand in hand with diversification, as in insurance underwriting.

questions.q: Graham argues that a sufficiently low price can turn a security of mediocre quality into a sound investment.
questions.why: Provided the buyer is informed and experienced and diversifies adequately. A low enough price creates the margin of safety that defines investment.

questions.q: Graham says that if the crowd disagrees with you, that is good evidence that your analysis is wrong.
questions.why: “You are neither right nor wrong because the crowd disagrees with you. You are right because your data and reasoning are right.”

questions.q: Graham ends: “To achieve satisfactory investment results is easier than most people realize; to achieve superior results is harder than it looks.”
questions.why: The typical investor can succeed by limiting ambition to capacity and keeping to the safe, narrow path of defensive investment.

questions.q: Peter Bernstein, drawing on Pascal’s wager, says that when deciding under uncertainty, the probabilities must dominate the consequences.
questions.why: The reverse: the consequences must dominate the probabilities, because we never know the future. You can’t control being wrong sometimes, but you can control what it costs.

questions.q: According to Graham, a true margin of safety is one that can be demonstrated by what?
options: Figures, persuasive reasoning and a body of actual experience
A strong market trend and the opinion of leading experts
Management’s forecasts and the analysts’ ratings of the share
Recent price momentum and unusually heavy trading volume
questions.why: To have a true investment there must be a true margin of safety. It is the touchstone that separates investment from speculation.

questions.q: Why does Graham doubt that speculators really enjoy a margin of safety, even when they feel the odds are in their favour?
options: Their claims rest on subjective judgment, unsupported by evidence or conclusive reasoning
Speculators seldom make money for long, so any margin they have soon disappears
Speculators nearly always use borrowed money, which wipes out any margin they might have
Their trades are too small and too short for any margin to build up in their favour
questions.why: Each feels the time is right, his skill superior or his system trustworthy. Betting on the market’s direction offers no safety margin in any useful sense.

questions.q: Why did Graham feel there were real risks in 1972, even in a diversified list of sound shares?
options: Typical earnings yields had fallen well below 9%, leaving too small an excess over bond interest
Companies had stopped raising their dividends, so share income no longer kept pace with prices
High-grade bonds were no longer available to individual investors at reasonable cost or yield
Diversification no longer worked, because all shares had begun to rise and fall together
questions.why: At 12 times earnings, the earnings yield was 8.33% against much higher bond rates than before. The old package of good profits and small risk was no longer available.

questions.q: When can an ordinary share offer a margin of safety as large as a good bond’s?
options: When a debt-free company sells for less than the bonds that could safely be issued against its assets and earnings
When it is a member of a major index, since the index funds then guarantee steady demand for it
When its dividend is higher than any bond’s coupon, so its income alone is better than a bond’s
When its price has risen for three years in a row, which shows the market is confident in the company’s future
questions.why: Many strong companies were in that position in 1932–33. The investor then gets a bond’s safety plus a share’s chances of gain.

questions.q: How does Graham link the margin of safety and diversification?
options: They work together: each holding has better odds of profit than loss, so many make an overall gain more certain
They are unrelated ideas, since one is about the price of a share and the other about the number held
Diversification replaces the need for a margin of safety, since losses on some shares are offset by others
A margin of safety makes diversification unnecessary, since each holding is safe enough on its own
questions.why: This is the simple basis of insurance underwriting. Without a margin, as in roulette, spreading bets only makes a loss more certain.

questions.q: What does the first business principle, “Know what you are doing; know your business”, mean for the investor?
options: Don’t aim for more than normal interest and dividends unless you know securities as well as a merchant knows his goods
Only buy shares in the company you work for, since that is the business you know best of all
Read the financial pages every day, so that you know what is happening in every market you are in
Always use a reputable broker, who knows the business of buying and selling securities far better than you do
questions.why: Investment is most intelligent when it is most businesslike. Buying and selling for profit is a business venture of your own.

questions.q: What does Graham’s third business principle mean for the enterprising investor?
options: Base operations on arithmetic, not optimism, and avoid ventures with little to gain and much to lose
Act on optimism when markets are rising, and on caution only when they are falling
Trade often to capture many small gains, since small profits add up over the years
Follow the calculations of trusted experts without checking them yourself, since they know more
questions.why: For every investor, if you accept a small return, as in a conventional bond, you must demand convincing evidence that you aren’t risking much of your principal.

questions.q: Which two factors does Daniel Kahneman say characterise good decisions?
options: Well-calibrated confidence and correctly anticipated regret
Speed in acting and boldness in the size of the bet
Expert advice and a strong record of recent performance
High conviction and a willingness to make concentrated bets
questions.why: Ask how well you really understand the investment, and how you will react if you are wrong. Zweig: risk is gazing back at you from the mirror.

questions.q: In the 1930s many real-estate bonds sold for under 10 cents on the dollar. What does Graham say about buying them then?
options: Many were attractive, reasonably safe investments, since true values were four or five times the price
They were pure speculation at any price, because real-estate bonds had already defaulted once
They should have been sold, since advisers and the rating agencies had turned against them
They were safe only at par, since a low price showed that the market expected a total loss
questions.why: The same bonds had been speculative at par in the 1920s, with little value above the debt. Price turned them into investments.

questions.q: Graham says the margin of safety for bonds can be measured in two ways. Which pair is right?
options: Earnings compared with interest charges, and the value of the business compared with its debt
The coupon compared with inflation, and the bond’s price compared with its par value
The credit rating compared with peers, and the bond’s maturity compared with its yield
The dividend compared with interest, and the company’s sales compared with its total debt
questions.why: Since average share prices track average earning power, both methods usually give similar results.

questions.q: A business owes R10m and is fairly worth R30m. How far could its value fall before bondholders lose money, in theory?
options: By two-thirds
By one-third
By 10%
questions.why: R30m − R10m = R20m of cushion, which is two-thirds of R30m. That cushion is the bondholders’ margin of safety.

questions.q: A railway earns its fixed charges five times over before tax. By roughly how much could its earnings fall before the balance after interest disappears?
questions.why: If earnings are 5 and interest 1, earnings can fall to 1, a drop of 4 ÷ 5 = 80%. That is the cushion Graham’s 5-times test provides.

questions.q: A share sells at 11 times earnings and bonds yield 4%. What is the share buyer’s annual margin, and about how much might it add up to over ten years?
options: About 5 points a year, roughly 50% of the price over ten years
About 7 points a year, roughly 70% of the price over ten years
About 11 points a year, roughly 110% of the price over ten years
None: the share yields less than the bond, so there is no margin
questions.why: 1 ÷ 11 ≈ 9% earnings yield, minus 4% = about 5 points. Graham says ten years of such excess may total about 50% of the price paid.

questions.q: You buy shares at 12 times earnings with a 4% dividend yield. What is the earnings yield, and how much of your cost is reinvested for you each year?
options: 8.33%, with 4.33% reinvested
12%, with 8% reinvested
8.33%, with 4% reinvested
4%, with nothing reinvested
questions.why: 1 ÷ 12 ≈ 8.33%, and 8.33% − 4% = 4.33%. Graham found this excess over 1972 bond yields too small to be an adequate margin.

questions.q: On a wheel with 38 numbers paying R35 profit on a R1 win, you bet R1 on every number. What happens each spin, and what if the payout were R39?
options: You lose R2 each spin; at R39 you would win R2 each spin
You win R35 each spin; at R39 you would win R39 each spin
You break even each spin, whichever of the payouts applies
You lose R1 each spin; at R39 you would win R1 each spin
questions.why: You win R35 on one number and lose R1 on 37: −R2. At R39 you would net +R2. With a negative margin, diversifying guarantees a loss; with a positive one, it guarantees a gain.

questions.q: A secondary company’s shares have an indicated value of R60. What is the most Graham would suggest paying as an unconventional investment?
options: R40: two-thirds or less of indicated value
R60: the full indicated value of the shares
R54: a 10% discount to the indicated value
R30: half of the indicated value, or less
questions.why: Two-thirds of R60 is R40. The R20 gap is the margin that absorbs miscalculations or worse-than-average luck.

questions.q: A company with no debt has a total market value of R43m and pre-tax earnings of R16m. If it borrowed R43m at 7%, how well would earnings cover the interest?
options: About 5.3 times: the shares carry a bond-like margin
About 2.7 times: below Graham’s standard for bonds
About 0.4 times: the interest couldn’t be paid at all
About 16 times: far above any standard Graham set
questions.why: Interest would be R43m × 7% ≈ R3m, and R16m ÷ R3m ≈ 5.3, above Graham’s 5-times standard. That was National Presto in 1972.

questions.q: Your share falls 50% in the first year and then gains 10% a year. Roughly how long does it take just to get back to where you started?
options: About 7 years
About 5 years
About 2 years
About 16 years
questions.why: You need to double, and 1.1⁷ ≈ 1.95. Overtaking a steady 5% a year takes over 16 years: the cost of paying too much at the outset.

questions.q: A share bought at R153.42 is now R2.47. At 10% a year, roughly how long would it take to get back to the purchase price?
options: About 43 years
About 10 years
About 62 years
About 6 years
questions.why: R153.42 ÷ R2.47 ≈ 62 times, and 1.1⁴³ ≈ 60. That was JDS Uniphase, bought at its March 2000 peak.

questions.q: An investor puts 85% of his money into one fashionable sector because he is sure it will rise. By Bernstein’s reading of Pascal’s wager, what is wrong with this?
options: He has ignored the consequences of being wrong, which should dominate the probabilities
His estimate of the probability that the sector will rise is far too low, not too high
He should have used borrowed money too, since his confidence in the sector is so high
Nothing: confidence in the outcome is enough to justify any concentration of money
questions.why: Nearly a tenth of investors surveyed in 1999 held at least 85% in internet shares. Diversification and refusing to overpay keep any mistake from being catastrophic.

questions.q: The two partners in Graham’s Postscript averaged about 20% a year on the capital they managed.
questions.why: They kept a widely diversified portfolio of more than a hundred issues and avoided anything that looked overpriced.

questions.q: The partners bought their half-interest in a company that Wall Street was eager to finance.
questions.why: The industry had no Wall Street appeal at the time, and several important houses had turned the deal down.

questions.q: Graham says the profits from that single investment far exceeded all the others made in 20 years of wide-ranging operations.
questions.why: Its share price rose two hundred times or more the price paid for the half-interest.

questions.q: Graham promises a similarly spectacular result to every intelligent investor who stays prudent and alert.
questions.why: He says plainly that he cannot. He won’t end with Raskob’s slogan “Everybody can be rich”, only with the promise of interesting possibilities.

questions.q: Zweig notes that Graham had established he could liquidate GEICO for at least what he paid for it.
questions.why: So the financial risk was small, even with about a quarter of the fund in one company. The risk he took was psychological.

questions.q: Zweig concludes that the GEICO story shows ordinary investors should put most of their money into one great company.
questions.why: The opposite. Since Graham himself called it a lucky break, the rest of us must diversify to keep investing from decaying into gambling.

questions.q: What was decisive for the partners in deciding to buy the half-interest?
options: The price was moderate in relation to current earnings and asset value
The industry was popular on Wall Street, which made a later sale easy
Other investment houses were competing to buy the same half-interest
Its share price had been rising fast, which confirmed its strong prospects
questions.why: They were impressed by its possibilities, but the deciding factor was value: the margin of safety at the price paid.

questions.q: The shares soon looked far too high by the partners’ own standards. Why did they keep a large holding?
options: They regarded the company as a sort of “family business”
They were legally barred from selling for several years
They expected a takeover bid at an even higher price
They thought it was still cheap by their own standards
questions.why: Many participants in their funds also held on and became millionaires through this one company and its later affiliates.

questions.q: What does Graham say usually lies behind the lucky break or the one supremely shrewd decision?
options: A background of preparation and disciplined capacity, plus the means, judgment and courage to act
Inside information that others don’t have, gained through close contacts with company managers
Pure chance and nothing else, since no amount of preparation can make the right opportunity appear
Following the crowd at exactly the right moment, then leaving just before everyone else does
questions.why: One must also be established enough for such opportunities to knock at one’s door. And can we tell luck and shrewdness apart?

questions.q: What does Zweig say about uncertainty and investing?
options: They are synonyms: uncertainty is permanent, and investing requires faith in a better tomorrow
Investors should wait until the uncertainty clears before committing new money to the market
Uncertainty exists only in bear markets; in bull markets the direction of prices is clear enough
Experts can remove most of the uncertainty with good forecasts, which is what investors pay them for
questions.why: No one has ever been able to see that a particular time is the best time to buy. Without faith in the future, no one would invest at all.

questions.q: Zweig says successful investing is about what?
options: Managing risk, not avoiding it
Avoiding all risk
Taking the biggest risks for the biggest gains
Predicting the market
questions.why: Graham’s large GEICO bet carried little financial risk thanks to its asset backing, though it took great courage psychologically.

questions.q: A fund puts R712,500 into one company, about 25% of its assets. Roughly how large is the fund?
options: About R2.85m
About R0.71m
About R1.78m
About R7.1m
questions.why: R712,500 ÷ 0.25 = R2.85m. Graham describes the stake as about a fifth of the fund; Zweig puts it at about 25%.

questions.q: A R11,413 holding grows to R1.66m over 24 years. Roughly what compound annual return is that?
options: About 23% a year
About 6% a year
About 14.5% a year
About 60% a year
questions.why: R1.66m ÷ R11,413 ≈ 145 times, and 145^(1/24) ≈ 1.23. That was a Graham-Newman holder who kept the GEICO shares from 1948 to 1972.

questions.q: A R712,500 half-interest later becomes worth 200 times the price paid. What is it worth?
options: About R142.5m
About R14.25m
About R71.25m
About R1.425bn
questions.why: R712,500 × 200 = R142.5m. The advance far outstripped the actual growth in profits.

questions.q: Bankers favour enterprise value multiples partly because they are independent of capital structure.
questions.why: They are also free of differences in tax regimes and some accounting policies, which affect net income and so P/E.

questions.q: Under the treasury stock method, the proceeds from exercising options are assumed to be used to repay debt.
questions.why: They are assumed to buy back shares at the current share price. The difference between options exercised and shares bought back is the net dilution.

questions.q: Options with an exercise price above the current share price are excluded from fully diluted shares.
questions.why: They are out of the money, so no holder would exercise them at today’s price.

questions.q: If a company borrows R100m and keeps the money as cash, its enterprise value rises by R100m.
questions.why: Debt rises by R100m and so does cash, so net debt and enterprise value are unchanged. Issuing equity to repay debt is also enterprise-value neutral.

questions.q: EBITDA is not a reported (GAAP) figure; it is usually built from EBIT plus D&A taken from the cash flow statement.
questions.why: It is widely used as a proxy for operating cash flow and as an apples-to-apples comparison across capital structures and tax regimes.

questions.q: P/E is the most useful multiple for valuing an early-stage company with little or no earnings to date.
questions.why: With tiny, zero or negative earnings, P/E is meaningless. EV/sales may be the meaningful reference point instead.

questions.q: Two companies with the same EBITDA margin can have quite different net income margins because of leverage and tax rates.
questions.why: Net income is after interest and tax, so it depends on capital structure and tax regime. Operating margins are not.

questions.q: To adjust net income for a pre-tax restructuring charge, add back the full pre-tax amount.
questions.why: Add back the full amount to EBIT and EBITDA, but tax-effect it for net income: add back the charge × (1 − tax rate).

questions.q: The multiple range finally selected is usually tighter than the universe’s high-to-low range.
questions.why: It leans on as few as two or three closest comparables, with the wider group as reference points.

questions.q: Out-of-the-money convertible bonds are added to fully diluted shares outstanding, just like in-the-money ones.
questions.why: They stay treated as debt. Only in-the-money convertibles are converted into shares.

questions.q: For mature listed companies EPS growth is usually more meaningful, while sales or EBITDA growth suits early-stage ones.
questions.why: Investors also ask whether growth is organic or acquisition-driven; organic growth is generally preferred.

questions.q: Credit rating agencies audit the financial statements of the companies they rate each year.
questions.why: Ratings are opinions on a borrower’s ability and willingness to pay in full and on time. Agencies do not conduct audits.

questions.q: In the book’s framework, which of these belongs to the financial profile rather than the business profile?
options: Return on investment
Distribution channels
Customers and end markets
Geography
questions.why: The financial profile covers size, profitability, growth, return on investment and credit. The business profile covers sector, products and services, customers and end markets, distribution channels and geography.

questions.q: Starting from scratch, where is usually the best place to begin looking for comparable companies?
options: The target’s listed competitors
Companies with the same share price
The largest companies in the market
Any company with similar EBITDA
questions.why: Competitors share key business and financial characteristics and similar opportunities and risks. Annual reports, research and industry codes then fill gaps.

questions.q: Why is the merger proxy for a recent deal in the sector a useful source of comparables?
options: Its fairness opinion excerpts list the comparable companies and multiple ranges used
It lists every listed company in the industry, along with each one’s market share
It gives the consensus estimates of the research analysts who cover the sector
It reports the credit ratings of the target and each of its main competitors
questions.why: The fairness opinion summarises the valuation work, typically comps, precedent transactions, DCF and, where relevant, LBO analysis.

questions.q: Why is EV/EBITDA generally preferred to EV/EBIT?
options: It isn’t distorted by depreciation differences from capex timing or by acquisition amortisation
EBIT is not a reported figure, so it has to be built from the notes for every company
EV/EBIT ignores the company’s debt, while EV/EBITDA takes the full capital structure into account
EV/EBITDA includes interest costs, so it reflects each company’s financing as well as its operations
questions.why: EV/EBIT can still help when D&A is unavailable, such as for divisions, or for very capital-intensive companies.

questions.q: Which of these pairings is inconsistent?
options: Enterprise value ÷ net income
Enterprise value ÷ EBITDA
Share price ÷ diluted EPS
Equity value ÷ net income
questions.why: Enterprise value belongs to debt and equity holders, so it pairs with sales, EBITDA or EBIT. Net income flows only to equity holders.

questions.q: A company trades at 55% of its 52-week high while its peers trade at 85–90% of theirs. What does this usually indicate?
options: Company-specific issues, such as missed guidance or management problems
A sector-wide downturn that has hit this company before its peers
That the company is cheap relative to its peers and should be bought
A pending share split, which has temporarily lowered its share price
questions.why: When one company is out of line with its peers, the cause is usually specific to it rather than to the sector.

questions.q: A generic drug maker is regularly sued over patent challenges. How should its legal costs be treated when scrubbing the financials?
options: Not necessarily as non-recurring: they are a normal part of its operations
As non-recurring in every case, so they are added back to EBITDA
As extraordinary gains, since the company usually wins its cases
Ignored entirely, since legal costs are not part of operating income
questions.why: What is one-off for one company can be routine for another. Bankers must use judgment, not labels alone.

questions.q: What is calendarisation for?
options: Aligning companies with different year-ends so that their multiples cover the same periods
Converting quarterly figures into monthly ones so that results can be tracked more closely
Adjusting every company’s historical figures for inflation so that the years are comparable
Removing seasonal effects from share prices so that the trading multiples are more stable
questions.why: Without it, multiples would be based on different periods and not truly comparable.

questions.q: Compared with the if-converted method, how does net share settlement treat an in-the-money convertible?
options: Face value stays as debt, settled in cash; only the excess of conversion value over par is paid in new shares
All of it becomes new shares at the conversion price, exactly as under the if-converted method
It is ignored until maturity, since the holder can still choose not to convert the bond at all
It is treated as preferred stock, so it is added to enterprise value but never to the share count
questions.why: So net share settlement issues fewer shares. As the share price rises, the excess, and so the new shares, grow.

questions.q: Which of these is a weakness of comparable companies analysis?
options: Valuations can be skewed by irrational exuberance or gloom, and pure-play peers may not exist
It relies only on management projections, which tend to be optimistic in a sale
It cannot be updated quickly, because share prices and estimates change too often
It ignores market sentiment, so it can value a company far from where it actually trades
questions.why: It may also be disconnected from the target’s cash flow and miss target-specific strengths and risks. Hence comps are used with other methods.

questions.q: A share trades at R40. There are 200m basic shares and 10m in-the-money options with an average exercise price of R30. What are fully diluted shares under the treasury stock method?
questions.why: Proceeds are 10m × R30 = R300m, buying back R300m ÷ R40 = 7.5m shares. Net new shares are 2.5m, so 200m + 2.5m = 202.5m.

questions.q: A share trades at R50. Tranche A: 2m options at R20. Tranche B: 1m options at R60. How many net new shares does the treasury stock method add?
options: 3m
2m
questions.why: Tranche B is out of the money and excluded. Tranche A raises R40m, buying back 0.8m shares, so net new shares are 2m − 0.8m = 1.2m.

questions.q: A R300m convertible has a conversion price of R25, and the share trades at R40. How many new shares does the if-converted method add?
options: None: it stays as debt
questions.why: It is in the money (R40 > R25), so R300m ÷ R25 = 12m shares, and the R300m is removed from debt.

questions.q: Same convertible (R300m at R25 conversion price, share at R40), but with net share settlement. How many new shares are issued?
options: 3m
questions.why: Conversion value is 12m × R40 = R480m. The R180m excess over par ÷ R40 = 4.5m shares. The R300m face value stays as debt.

questions.q: Equity value is R4,000m, debt R1,500m, preferred stock R100m, noncontrolling interest R50m and cash R250m. What is enterprise value?
Sales were R2,000m for the last financial year. Nine-month sales are R1,600m this year against R1,450m for the same nine months last year. What are LTM sales?
questions.why: LTM = prior year + current stub − prior stub = R2,000m + R1,600m − R1,450m = R2,150m.

questions.q: A company’s year ends in March. Sales are R1,200m for the year to March 2026 and forecast at R1,320m for the year to March 2027. What are calendar 2026 sales?
questions.why: Calendar 2026 has 3 months from the year to March 2026 and 9 from the next: (3/12 × R1,200m) + (9/12 × R1,320m) = R300m + R990m = R1,290m.

questions.q: Reported net income is R150m after a R30m pre-tax restructuring charge you judge non-recurring. The tax rate is 27%. What is adjusted net income?
options: About R171.9m
R180m
About R158.1m
R150m
questions.why: R30m × (1 − 0.27) = R21.9m added back, giving R171.9m. Adding the full R30m is the classic error.

questions.q: The selected range is 6.0× to 7.0× EBITDA of R500m. Net debt is R800m and there are 100m fully diluted shares. What is the implied share price range?
options: R22 to R27
R30 to R35
R38 to R43
R14 to R19
questions.why: EV is R3,000m to R3,500m. Less R800m net debt gives equity of R2,200m to R2,700m, or R22 to R27 a share.

questions.q: A P/E range of 10× to 12× is applied to net income of R180m. With net debt of R600m, what is the implied enterprise value range?
questions.why: Equity value is R1,800m to R2,160m. Adding net debt of R600m gives R2,400m to R2,760m.

questions.q: A company has debt of R1,200m, cash of R120m, LTM EBITDA of R480m and interest of R60m. What are total leverage, net leverage and EBITDA interest cover?
A company pays a quarterly dividend of R0.75 and its share trades at R60. What is the implied dividend yield?
questions.why: Annualise first: R0.75 × 4 = R3.00, and R3.00 ÷ R60 = 5%. Using the quarterly figure alone gives the 1.25% trap.

questions.q: Diluted EPS rose from R2.00 to R2.42 over two years. What is the compound annual growth rate?
questions.why: (R2.42 ÷ R2.00)^(1/2) − 1 = 1.21^0.5 − 1 = 10%. Dividing the 21% total by two (10.5%) ignores compounding.

questions.q: Under normal market conditions, transaction comps tend to give a higher multiple range than trading comps.
questions.why: Buyers usually pay a control premium, and strategic buyers can often pay more because of expected synergies.

questions.q: Older transactions are generally more relevant than recent ones, because their outcomes are known.
questions.why: Deals from the last two to three years are usually most relevant, since they happened in similar market conditions. Older deals can help only if they occurred at a similar point in the cycle.

questions.q: Strategic buyers have traditionally been able to pay higher prices than financial sponsors.
questions.why: They may realise synergies and often have a lower cost of capital and return thresholds. In credit booms, sponsors’ higher leverage narrows the gap.

questions.q: Deals paid largely in the acquirer’s shares tend to show higher multiples and premiums than all-cash deals.
questions.why: They tend to show lower ones. Target holders keep a stake in the upside and synergies, and can still get a control premium later, so they accept less up front.

questions.q: With a fixed exchange ratio, the number of shares received is fixed, but their value moves with the acquirer’s share price.
questions.why: Both sides share the risk and opportunity of price moves after announcement. It is the more common structure.

questions.q: With a floating exchange ratio, the target’s shareholders bear the risk of a fall in the acquirer’s share price.
questions.why: The value per share is fixed, so the acquirer bears that risk by issuing more shares if its price falls.

questions.q: For precedent transactions, all in-the-money options are counted in fully diluted shares, whether or not they have vested.
questions.why: Unvested options typically vest on a change of control. Out-of-the-money options are still excluded.

questions.q: Transaction multiples are normally calculated on the projections the acquirer used to set its price.
questions.why: Those projections are usually confidential. Multiples are based on actual LTM figures available at announcement.

questions.q: A premiums paid analysis applies only where the target is a listed company.
questions.why: A premium needs a market share price to measure against, so it doesn’t apply to private targets.

questions.q: The share price on the day before the deal announcement is always the right base for measuring the premium.
questions.why: If there were leaks, rumours or a “strategic alternatives” announcement, that price is not unaffected. Measure from before the leak, at several intervals.

questions.q: Transaction multiples are usually shown on reported LTM figures without synergies, though synergy-adjusted ones may be added.
questions.why: Adjusted multiples add full run-rate cost synergies (excluding costs to achieve) to EBITDA or EPS to show what the buyer effectively paid.

questions.q: A merger of equals typically carries a large takeover premium for the target’s shareholders.
questions.why: It is premised on partnership: the typical premium is forgone as both sides share the upside from growth and synergies over time.

questions.q: What are the two main reasons transaction multiples tend to exceed trading multiples?
options: A control premium, and synergies that strategic buyers expect to realise
Higher interest rates at the time of the deal, and the tax savings on debt
Lower trading volumes in the target’s shares, and accounting differences
Analyst optimism about the sector, and share buybacks by listed companies
questions.why: In return for the premium, the buyer controls the business and its cash flows. Synergies add value beyond the target’s stand-alone results.

questions.q: For which kind of deal is it hardest to find reliable deal information?
options: A private buyer acquiring a private target with non-public financing
A listed buyer acquiring a listed target, paid for with its own shares
A listed buyer issuing registered shares to pay for a private target
An LBO funded with registered high-yield bonds sold to the public
questions.why: There are no disclosure requirements, so the banker relies on press releases, news and trade journals, and some deals can’t be used at all.

questions.q: A corporation that needs cash sells a non-core division. How might this affect the price?
options: It may accept a lower value in exchange for speed and certainty of completion
It will demand the highest possible price, since it needs every rand it can get
It has no effect on the price, since buyers only look at the division’s results
The buyer must pay a higher control premium to persuade the board to sell
questions.why: Seller motivations matter. Equally, a buyer may “stretch” for an asset with big synergies or scarcity value.

questions.q: Why would a high-multiple LBO won at auction in the mid-2000s credit boom be less relevant for valuing a company in 2009?
options: Debt was abundant and cheap then, but scarce and expensive afterwards, changing what buyers could pay
LBOs never provide useful multiples, because sponsors pay less than strategic buyers do for the same assets
Auctions always produce prices below fair value, so the multiples from that time understate value
The accounting rules for LBOs were different then, so the reported EBITDA figures can’t be compared
questions.why: Market conditions directly affect the availability and cost of financing, and so the price buyers will or can pay.

questions.q: When is a floating exchange ratio typically used?
options: When the acquirer is much larger than the target
When the target is much larger than the acquirer
When the deal is all cash
When both companies are private
questions.why: A slump in a small target barely affects a big acquirer, but the reverse isn’t true, which justifies giving the target a fixed value.

questions.q: In a fixed exchange ratio deal, what does a collar do?
options: Guarantees the target’s holders a value within a set range, whatever the acquirer’s shares do
Fixes the acquirer’s share price at its level on the day the deal is announced
Caps the number of new shares the acquirer can issue to complete the transaction
Prevents rival bidders from making an offer until the shareholders have voted on the deal
questions.why: For example, an offer worth R20 a share might be guaranteed to deliver between R18 and R22 between signing and closing.

questions.q: Precedent transactions imply a valuation well below trading comps. What should the banker do?
options: Recheck both peer sets and the calculations, though it can be valid if the sector is at a cyclical high or “in play”
Use the lower figure without question, since precedent transactions reflect real prices actually paid
Discard the precedent transactions entirely, since comps are always the more reliable of the two methods
Average the two valuations and move on, since the differences between methods tend to cancel each other out
questions.why: Normally precedents sit above comps because of control premiums, so a big gap the other way is a red flag worth checking.

questions.q: In a tender offer, which document contains the target board’s recommendation to its shareholders?
options: Schedule 14D-9
Schedule TO
Form 10-Q
Schedule 13E-3
questions.why: The acquirer files the Schedule TO; the target responds with the 14D-9, typically including a fairness opinion.

questions.q: The universe’s mean is 7.5× LTM EBITDA, but the three most relevant deals were done at 8.0× to 8.5×. Which range best follows the book’s approach?
questions.why: The range leans on the best transactions while keeping the wider universe in view.

questions.q: Which of these is a weakness of precedent transactions?
options: A time lag: past deals may not reflect today’s conditions
It ignores the actual prices that buyers paid for targets
It always requires the target’s management projections
It cannot be used to value companies in M&A situations
questions.why: Other weaknesses: few truly comparable deals, limited information, and prices that rest on undisclosed projections rather than LTM figures.

questions.q: An acquirer offers 0.6 of its shares for each target share. The acquirer trades at R50, and the target has 40m fully diluted shares. What are the offer price per share and the equity value?
options: R30 a share and R1,200m
R50 a share and R2,000m
R30 a share and R2,000m
R83 a share and R3,333m
questions.why: 0.6 × R50 = R30, and R30 × 40m = R1,200m. The acquirer issues 0.6 × 40m = 24m shares.

questions.q: In that fixed-ratio deal (0.6 shares for each of 40m target shares), the acquirer’s shares fall to R45 before closing, with no collar. What do target holders now receive?
options: Still 24m shares in total, now worth R27 per target share
More shares in total, so the value stays at R30 a share
R30 in cash per share, since the offer value was fixed
Nothing changes in value, since the ratio is unchanged
questions.why: The share count is fixed, so value falls: 0.6 × R45 = R27. Target holders bear the risk, and keep the upside.

questions.q: Under a floating exchange ratio, target holders are to receive R30 of acquirer shares each. How many acquirer shares does each get if the acquirer trades at R40, and at R50?
options: 0.75 at R40 and 0.6 at R50
0.6 at R40 and 0.75 at R50
0.75 either way
1.33 at R40 and 1.67 at R50
questions.why: R30 ÷ R40 = 0.75 and R30 ÷ R50 = 0.6. The value is fixed; the number of shares floats.

questions.q: An offer gives R12 in cash plus 0.3 acquirer shares (trading at R40) for each of the target’s 50m shares. What is the equity value?
options: R1,200m: R24 a share
R600m
R720m: R14.40 a share
R2,600m: R52 a share
questions.why: R12 + 0.3 × R40 = R24, and R24 × 50m = R1,200m: R600m in cash and 15m new shares.

questions.q: A target trades at R23.50 the day before announcement, but was R20.00 before rumours of a sale began. The offer is R26.00. What are the premiums to each price?
options: About 10.6% to the day before, and 30% to the unaffected price
30% to the day before, and about 10.6% to the unaffected price
About 10.6% to both the day-before and unaffected prices
R2.50 to the day before, and R6.00 to the unaffected price
questions.why: R26.00 ÷ R23.50 − 1 ≈ 10.6%, and R26.00 ÷ R20.00 − 1 = 30%. The unaffected premium isolates the true effect of the offer.

questions.q: The offer is R25 a share. The target has 80m basic shares and 4m options with an average exercise price of R10, some still unvested. What is the equity purchase price?
options: About R2,060m
About R2,040m
questions.why: All in-the-money options count: proceeds R40m buy back 1.6m shares at R25, so net new shares are 2.4m. 82.4m × R25 = R2,060m.

questions.q: The equity purchase price is R2,500m. The target has debt of R1,400m and cash of R100m, and LTM EBITDA of R475m. What is the EV/LTM EBITDA multiple?
questions.why: Enterprise value = R2,500m + R1,400m − R100m = R3,800m, and R3,800m ÷ R475m = 8.0×.

questions.q: A deal values the target at R3,600m, or 9.0× LTM EBITDA of R400m. The buyer expects R80m of annual run-rate cost synergies. What is the synergy-adjusted multiple?
questions.why: R3,600m ÷ (R400m + R80m) = 7.5×. It shows the effective price after the synergies the buyer expects to capture.

questions.q: A buyer pays R1,600m for 80% of a company’s shares. What equity value is implied for the whole company?
questions.why: Gross it up: R1,600m ÷ 0.8 = R2,000m. Multiples must be on a 100% basis to be comparable.

questions.q: A selected range of 7.5× to 8.5× is applied to LTM EBITDA of R600m for a private company with net debt of R1,000m. What equity value range is implied?
questions.why: Enterprise value is R4,500m to R5,100m. For a private target, equity value = enterprise value − net debt: R3,500m to R4,100m.

questions.q: The value a DCF produces is called intrinsic value, as distinct from the market value at a given moment.
questions.why: That is why a DCF is a useful check on market-based methods, which can be distorted by bubbles or credit crunches.

questions.q: Unlevered free cash flow is calculated after paying interest expense on the company’s debt.
questions.why: It is before interest: the cash available to all capital providers, debt and equity alike. That makes it independent of capital structure.

questions.q: An increase in net working capital is a use of cash and reduces free cash flow.
questions.why: A growing company typically ties up more cash in receivables and inventory. A decrease in NWC is a source of cash.

questions.q: An increase in accounts payable is a use of cash, because the company owes its suppliers more.
questions.why: It is a source of cash: money kept rather than paid out. Companies try to push out their DPO, within reason.

questions.q: Depreciation and amortisation reduce reported earnings but are added back when calculating free cash flow.
questions.why: They are non-cash expenses. Capex, by contrast, is an actual cash outflow and is subtracted.

questions.q: Adding more debt to a capital structure lowers WACC without limit, because interest is tax-deductible.
questions.why: WACC falls only up to the optimal capital structure. Beyond it, the cost of possible financial distress outweighs the tax benefit, and WACC rises.

questions.q: Under CAPM, equity investors are compensated for systematic risk but not for unsystematic (company-specific) risk.
questions.why: Unsystematic risk can be diversified away, so the market pays no premium for bearing it.

questions.q: A share with a beta below 1.0 has more systematic risk than the market as a whole.
questions.why: Below 1.0 means less systematic risk and so a lower cost of equity; above 1.0 means more.

questions.q: Using the mid-year convention gives a slightly higher value than year-end discounting.
questions.why: It assumes cash arrives evenly through the year, so on average it is received sooner.

questions.q: A terminal value from the exit multiple method is discounted using the mid-year convention.
questions.why: The exit multiple method uses year-end discounting, since it is based on year-end trading multiples. Under mid-year discounting, the perpetuity growth method uses mid-year.

questions.q: The terminal year should reflect a normalised, steady-state level of performance, not a cyclical high or low.
questions.why: Because the terminal value is such a large share of value, an unrepresentative final year would skew the whole valuation.

questions.q: The cost of debt is used before tax in the WACC formula, without any adjustment for the tax shield.
questions.why: It is tax-effected, r(d) × (1 − t), because interest payments are tax-deductible.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT deducted (or added) in moving from EBIT to unlevered free cash flow?
options: Interest expense
Taxes on EBIT
Capital expenditure
Increase in net working capital
questions.why: FCF = EBIT − taxes + D&A − capex − increase in NWC. Interest belongs to debt holders and is left out.

questions.q: When might a projection period much longer than five years be appropriate?
options: For an early-stage, fast-growing company, or one with long-term contracted revenue such as a utility
For any mature company in a stable sector, since its cash flows are easier to forecast far ahead
Whenever the WACC is high, since a longer period reduces the weight of the terminal value
When the company carries a lot of debt that will have to be repaid over more than five years
questions.why: The aim is to project until the business reaches a steady state that can support the terminal value.

questions.q: How do bankers usually estimate beta for a private company?
options: Unlever the betas of listed peers, average them, then relever at the target’s capital structure
Use a beta of 1.0, since a private company’s shares can’t be compared with the market
Use the beta of the largest listed company in the sector, as the best-known benchmark
Average the peers’ levered betas without adjustment, since they already include leverage
questions.why: Unlevering strips out each peer’s leverage; relevering applies the target’s own D/E and tax rate.

questions.q: Why do many bankers prefer a predicted beta to a historical one?
options: Past returns may not reliably show future risk, and predicted betas are meant to look forward
Historical betas can’t be used in published valuations under the regulators’ current rules
Predicted betas are always lower, which raises the valuation the seller is hoping for
Historical betas ignore the market and measure only the share’s own price movements
questions.why: Historical beta looks back over two to five years. What matters for the cost of equity is expected risk.

questions.q: Why might a banker add a size premium to the CAPM cost of equity?
options: Smaller companies appear riskier, and limited trading means beta may not fully capture that risk
Larger companies grow faster, so smaller ones need a premium to make up for slower growth
Regulators require it for any company with a market value below a set level of capitalisation
It reduces the cost of equity for smaller companies, which lifts their valuation to fair levels
questions.why: The evidence suggests smaller companies earn higher returns. The premium, tiered by market capitalisation, adds that risk.

questions.q: What target capital structure is typically used when calculating WACC for a private company?
options: The mean or median of its comparable companies
Its current capital structure, whatever it is
100% equity, since private firms rarely borrow
The structure that carries the most debt possible
questions.why: For a listed company, the existing structure is used if it is comfortably within the peer range. It is then held constant throughout the projection period.

questions.q: The perpetuity growth rate implied by your exit multiple is 7%. What does that suggest?
options: The exit multiple may be unrealistically high
The WACC is too high
The projections are too conservative
Nothing: any implied growth rate is acceptable
questions.why: Long-term growth is typically about 2–4%, roughly nominal GDP growth. Each method should sanity-check the other.

questions.q: Why do bankers often assume depreciation and capex converge by the final projection year?
options: So the asset base stays steady in perpetuity, as befits a steady-state business
To increase the valuation by lowering the capex in the terminal year
Because the tax rules require depreciation to equal capital spending
To reduce working capital needs in the final year of the projection
questions.why: Otherwise the terminal value would reflect an endlessly growing or shrinking asset base.

questions.q: Which of these is a weakness of DCF analysis?
options: Its value can rest largely on the terminal value and is very sensitive to small changes in assumptions
It ignores cash flow and relies only on accounting earnings, which can be managed by companies
It depends entirely on comparable companies, so it fails when there are no listed peers to use
It cannot model different scenarios, so it gives only a single answer for the company’s value
questions.why: It also depends on accurate forecasts and assumes a constant capital structure. Its strengths: cash-flow based, market-independent, self-sufficient and flexible.

questions.q: A company has very different business segments. What approach does the book suggest?
options: A sum-of-the-parts DCF: value each segment with its own WACC and add them up
Use the WACC of the largest segment for all of them, for consistency
Average the segments’ growth rates and value the company as one unit
Ignore the smaller segments, since they barely move the overall value
questions.why: Segments with different risks deserve different costs of capital.

questions.q: EBIT is R500m and the tax rate 27%. D&A is R120m, capex R150m, and net working capital rises by R35m. What is unlevered free cash flow?
options: R300m
R335m
R435m
R230m
questions.why: EBIAT = R500m × 0.73 = R365m. Then R365m + R120m − R150m − R35m = R300m.

questions.q: Net working capital is R600m this year and is projected at R640m next year. What is the effect on next year’s free cash flow?
options: It reduces FCF by R40m (a use of cash)
It increases FCF by R40m (a source of cash)
It reduces FCF by R640m (the full balance)
No effect, since working capital isn’t cash
questions.why: Only the change matters: R640m − R600m = R40m more cash tied up in working capital.

questions.q: Accounts receivable are R123m on annual sales of R1,000m. What is DSO, using a 365-day year?
options: About 45 days
About 123 days
About 8 days
About 30 days
questions.why: R123m ÷ R1,000m × 365 ≈ 45 days: on average, customers pay 45 days after the sale.

questions.q: Inventory is R240m and cost of goods sold is R1,095m. What are days inventory held and inventory turns?
options: About 80 days and about 4.6 turns
About 4.6 days and 80 turns
About 22 days and about 16.5 turns
About 80 days and about 0.2 turns
questions.why: DIH = R240m ÷ R1,095m × 365 = 80 days. Turns = R1,095m ÷ R240m ≈ 4.6 a year. Note that inventory is measured against COGS, not sales.

questions.q: The risk-free rate is 10%, levered beta 1.1 and the market risk premium 6%. What is the CAPM cost of equity?
questions.why: 10% + 1.1 × 6% = 16.6%. Multiplying the risk-free rate by beta as well is a common slip.

questions.q: Debt is 30% of total capitalisation, the pre-tax cost of debt 11%, the tax rate 27% and the cost of equity 16%. What is WACC?
options: About 13.6%
About 14.5%, using the pre-tax cost of debt
About 10.4%, with the weights swapped

questions.q: A peer has a levered beta of 1.35, a debt-to-equity ratio of 50% and a tax rate of 27%. What is its unlevered beta?
options: About 0.99
About 1.35
About 0.90
About 1.84

questions.q: The peers’ average unlevered beta is 1.0. Relever it at a target debt-to-equity of 40% and a tax rate of 27%.
options: About 1.29
About 0.77

questions.q: Terminal-year FCF is R450m, the perpetuity growth rate 4% and WACC 12%. What is the terminal value by the perpetuity growth method?
questions.why: TV = FCF × (1 + g) ÷ (WACC − g) = R450m × 1.04 ÷ 0.08 = R5,850m. Forgetting to grow FCF by a year gives R5,625m.

questions.q: Terminal-year EBITDA (year 5) is R900m, the exit multiple 7.5× and WACC 10%. What is the present value of the terminal value, discounting at year-end?
options: About R4,191m
About R4,396m
About R6,136m
questions.why: TV = R900m × 7.5 = R6,750m, and R6,750m ÷ 1.10⁵ = R6,750m ÷ 1.611 ≈ R4,191m. Mid-year discounting (about R4,396m) is the trap for the exit multiple method.

questions.q: A DCF gives an enterprise value of R5,900m. The company has debt of R1,500m, cash of R250m and noncontrolling interest of R100m. What is implied equity value?
The present value of projected FCF is R1,600m and of the terminal value R4,300m. What share of enterprise value comes from the terminal value?
options: About 73%
About 37%
About 27%
About 269%
questions.why: R4,300m ÷ (R1,600m + R4,300m) = R4,300m ÷ R5,900m ≈ 73%. That is typical, and why terminal assumptions deserve scrutiny.

questions.q: At a 10% discount rate, what are the year-end and mid-year discount factors for year one?
options: About 0.909 and about 0.953
About 0.953 and about 0.909
questions.why: Year-end: 1 ÷ 1.10 ≈ 0.909. Mid-year: 1 ÷ 1.10^0.5 ≈ 0.953. The mid-year factor is higher because the cash arrives sooner.

questions.q: Sponsors have historically sought annual returns of 20% or more and an exit within about five years.
questions.why: The threshold can move with market conditions and the risk of the deal, but 20%+ has been the rule of thumb.

questions.q: In a traditional LBO, the sponsor’s equity makes up 60% to 70% of the financing, with debt the rest.
questions.why: Debt has typically been 60–70%, with equity 30–40%. In tight markets like 2009, equity rose towards half.

questions.q: IRR reflects the time value of money, while the cash return (multiple of money) does not.
questions.why: The same proceeds received sooner produce a higher IRR; the multiple is unchanged.

questions.q: Bank debt is usually the most expensive form of LBO financing, because banks demand the highest coupons.
questions.why: It is usually the cheapest: secured, senior and shorter-dated. The price is less flexibility, with collateral and maintenance covenants.

questions.q: A revolving credit facility can be drawn, repaid and drawn again, whereas a term loan cannot be reborrowed once repaid.
questions.why: The revolver provides ongoing liquidity and is usually undrawn at close; lenders earn a commitment fee on the unused part.

questions.q: High yield bonds typically carry financial maintenance covenants tested every quarter.
questions.why: They have incurrence covenants, which bite only when the issuer takes an action such as borrowing more or paying a dividend. Bank debt has the maintenance covenants.

questions.q: Debt at the operating company is structurally senior to holding company debt, unless the operating company guarantees the latter.
questions.why: The assets sit in the operating company, whose creditors must be paid in full before anything flows up to its shareholder.

questions.q: Traditional first lien bank debt usually has strict call protection, with penalties for early repayment.
questions.why: It can normally be repaid at any time without penalty. Call protection is standard for high yield bonds.

questions.q: In a dividend recapitalisation, the sponsor takes cash out while keeping 100% of its ownership.
questions.why: The company borrows more to pay a dividend. The sponsor can still sell or list later, and may recoup all its original equity.

questions.q: A bridge loan is normally intended to be drawn and held by the banks for the long term.
questions.why: It is a last resort, giving the seller certainty of funding if bonds can’t be sold by closing. It is costly and is meant to stay unfunded.

questions.q: Holding exit value fixed, more debt and a smaller equity cheque raise the sponsor’s returns, but also the company’s risk.
questions.why: Interest is tax-deductible too, but higher leverage raises the chance of financial distress and cuts flexibility.

questions.q: Maintenance capex can be cut back in a downturn, whereas growth capex can’t be reduced at all.
questions.why: The reverse: maintenance capex sustains existing assets and is needed to keep operating; growth capex is discretionary.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a typical feature of a strong LBO candidate?
options: Heavy, ongoing capital spending needs
Strong, predictable cash flow
A leading, defensible market position
A proven management team
questions.why: Low capex leaves more cash for debt service. Growth and efficiency opportunities and a strong asset base also help.

questions.q: Why does a strong asset base help an LBO?
options: It gives lenders collateral and comfort on recovery, opening up more bank debt, the cheapest kind
It raises the company’s P/E ratio, so the sponsor can sell the business for more at exit
It removes the need for covenants, since lenders can simply seize the assets if payments stop
It means little or no equity is needed, since the assets alone can secure the whole price
questions.why: Receivables and inventory are especially valued for their liquidity. Still, an asset-light company can qualify if its cash flow is strong.

questions.q: How does an institutional Term Loan B typically differ from a Term Loan A?
options: Nominal amortisation (about 1% a year), a bullet at maturity, a longer tenor and institutional lenders
Heavy amortisation and a shorter tenor, since it is held mainly by the arranging commercial banks
It is unsecured and pays a fixed rate, so it ranks behind the revolver and Term Loan A in a default
It can be repaid and drawn again during its life, like a revolver, but with a longer final maturity
questions.why: Institutional investors prefer longer, non-amortising loans with higher coupons; banks prefer the TLA to mature first.

questions.q: What does mezzanine debt typically offer investors?
options: A higher return than high yield bonds, often mixing cash and PIK interest, sometimes with warrants
First lien security over all the assets and the lowest coupon of any layer in the structure
Daily liquidity, since mezzanine debt trades on an exchange like ordinary listed bonds do
A guaranteed return of capital, since the sponsor must repay it before taking any dividends
questions.why: It sits between debt and equity and is highly negotiated. For sponsors it is cheaper than equity when other debt isn’t available.

questions.q: How does an incurrence covenant work?
options: It blocks actions such as new debt or dividends only if the issuer would then fail a ratio test and lack a basket
It requires the issuer to meet set financial ratios at the end of every single quarter, whatever actions it takes
It bans all dividends to the sponsor for as long as any of the bonds remain outstanding
It lets lenders approve the share price at which the sponsor may later sell the company
questions.why: Maintenance covenants, typical of bank debt, must be met every quarter, with leverage limits that step down over time.

questions.q: Why do sponsors usually want management to roll over or invest equity?
options: To align management’s incentives with the sponsor’s in creating value
To reduce the amount of debt needed to finance the purchase
Because lenders won’t provide the debt unless management invests
To avoid paying management salaries during the holding period
questions.why: Broad equity incentives tied to targets are often a key difference from public-company ownership.

questions.q: What does a change of control put in a bond indenture give bondholders?
options: The right to require the issuer to buy back the bonds at 101% of par if ownership changes
The right to convert their bonds into shares of the new owner at a set conversion price
A higher coupon each year until the new owner repays the bonds in full at maturity
Control of the board until the new owner has refinanced all of the existing bonds
questions.why: It protects bondholders from a new owner with a riskier plan.

questions.q: Why have sponsors traditionally preferred to sell portfolio companies to strategic buyers?
options: Strategic buyers can often pay more, thanks to synergies and a lower cost of capital
Strategic buyers never use debt, so the deal is far more certain to close on time
IPOs are prohibited for sponsor-owned companies under most stock exchange rules
Strategic buyers also take over the sponsor’s fund and its other portfolio companies
questions.why: In strong debt markets, rival sponsors can compete on price, so sales to other sponsors have grown.

questions.q: A sponsor puts in 30% of the purchase price as equity. What comfort does this give lenders?
options: The business’s value would have to fall by more than 30% before their principal is at risk
Their loans are guaranteed by the sponsor up to 30% of the purchase price if the deal fails
Interest will always be paid, since the sponsor must cover any shortfall from its own fund
They own 30% of the company’s equity, so they share in any gain the sponsor makes at exit
questions.why: Equity is wiped out before debt holders lose value. It acts as a cushion beneath the debt.

questions.q: Which company could usually support the highest leverage?
options: A subscription business with highly visible cash flows
A highly cyclical steel producer at the top of its cycle
An early-stage company with fast but volatile sales
A company in a sector that is at a cyclical peak
questions.why: Markets and rating agencies take a more conservative view of leverage in cyclical sectors, to survive the troughs.

questions.q: A sponsor invests R300m of equity and receives R1,000m after five years, with nothing in between. What are the cash return and IRR, roughly?
options: About 3.3× and about 27%
About 3.3× and about 47%
About 2.3× and about 18%
About 3.3× and about 67%
questions.why: R1,000m ÷ R300m ≈ 3.33×, and 3.33^(1/5) − 1 ≈ 27.2%. Dividing the 233% gain by five (47%) ignores compounding.

questions.q: A sponsor buys a company for R1,000m with R700m of debt and R300m of equity. Over five years R500m of debt is repaid, and the company is sold for R1,000m. What is the equity worth, and the cash return?
options: R800m: about 2.7×
R1,000m: about 3.3×
R500m: about 1.7×
questions.why: Debt falls to R200m, so equity = R1,000m − R200m = R800m. Debt repayment raises equity value rand for rand, with no growth in enterprise value.

questions.q: Two ways to buy a R1,000m company and sell it for R1,500m after five years: (A) R700m equity, all R300m of debt repaid; (B) R300m equity, R700m debt cut to about R506m. Which gives the higher cash return?
options: B: about R994m on R300m, about 3.3×, against about 2.1× for A
A: R1,500m on R700m, about 2.1×, against about 1.7× for B
Both give the same return, since the exit value is the same
A: it has no debt left at exit, so its return is the higher
questions.why: A: R1,500m ÷ R700m ≈ 2.1×. B: (R1,500m − R506m) ÷ R300m ≈ 3.3×. Leverage boosts returns despite the extra interest.

questions.q: A R400m revolver charges a 0.5% annual commitment fee on the undrawn amount. Average usage is R100m. What is the annual commitment fee?
options: R1.5m
R2.0m
R0.5m
R4.0m
questions.why: (R400m − R100m) × 0.5% = R1.5m. The drawn R100m pays interest at the benchmark rate plus a spread instead.

questions.q: An asset-based facility of R300m lends 85% against eligible receivables of R200m and 60% against eligible inventory of R150m. How much can be borrowed?
options: R260m
R300m
R350m
R170m
questions.why: Borrowing base = R170m + R90m = R260m. Availability is the lesser of the base and the R300m commitment.

questions.q: A term loan pays the benchmark rate plus 4.0%, with a 1.5% floor on the benchmark. What is the coupon if the benchmark is 0.5%, and if it is 2.0%?
questions.why: Below the floor, the floor applies: 1.5% + 4.0% = 5.5%. Above it, 2.0% + 4.0% = 6.0%.

questions.q: An 8-year bond with an 8% coupon is non-callable for four years, then callable at par plus half the coupon, stepping down. At what price can it first be called?
questions.why: Par plus half the 8% coupon = 104. A year later par plus a quarter (102), then par.

questions.q: A 10% high yield bond has an equity clawback. If the issuer lists within three years, how much can it redeem, and at what price?
options: Up to 35% of the bonds, at 110
All of the bonds, at par (100)
Up to 35% of the bonds, at 101
Up to 10% of the bonds, at 135
questions.why: The clawback typically allows up to 35% to be redeemed with IPO proceeds at par plus the coupon.

questions.q: A buyout uses R400m more debt at 8% interest. With a 27% tax rate, what is the extra after-tax interest cost in the first year?
options: About R23.4m
R32m
About R8.6m
R40m
questions.why: R400m × 8% = R32m pre-tax, and R32m × (1 − 0.27) ≈ R23.4m. That is less cash available to repay debt.

questions.q: A R1bn fund charges a 2% management fee and 20% carried interest. In one year it earns R500m of profit above its required returns. What do the general partners receive?
options: R20m in fees plus R100m of carry
R20m in fees only
R100m in fees plus R20m of carry
R200m in total
questions.why: Fee: 2% × R1bn = R20m. Carry: 20% × R500m = R100m.

questions.q: A company with EBITDA of R100m is bought at 8.0× EBITDA, with debt of 5.0× EBITDA. What share of the price is equity?
questions.why: Price R800m, debt R500m, equity R300m: R300m ÷ R800m = 37.5%, within the traditional 30–40% range.

questions.q: Debt financing fees are capitalised and amortised, while other deal fees are expensed and reduce the equity contributed.
questions.why: Amortisation of financing fees is a non-cash charge, added back on the cash flow statement.

questions.q: In a sources and uses table, the total sources may be less than the total uses, with the gap left unfunded.
questions.why: Sources must always equal uses: every rand spent on the purchase, refinancing and fees must be funded.

questions.q: Under a 100% cash flow sweep, excess free cash flow repays prepayable bank debt, but high yield notes are left untouched.
questions.why: The notes have call protection and no amortisation, so they stay outstanding until refinanced or repaid at maturity.

questions.q: LBO models usually calculate each year’s interest on the ending debt balance rather than the average.
questions.why: They usually use the average of the beginning and ending balances, since bank debt is repaid through the year.

questions.q: Average-balance interest creates a circular reference in the model, which needs Excel’s iteration setting.
questions.why: Interest affects net income and cash for repayment, which affects ending debt, which affects interest.

questions.q: To be conservative, LBO analysis usually assumes an exit multiple above the entry multiple.
questions.why: Common practice is an exit multiple equal to, or below, the entry multiple. Multiple expansion is a hoped-for bonus, not the base case.

questions.q: With a fixed exit multiple, later exit years tend to show a rising cash return but a falling IRR.
questions.why: Equity value keeps growing as debt is repaid, but slower growth and the time value of money pull the annual return down.

questions.q: LBO analysis typically produces the highest valuation range of all the methods on the football field.
questions.why: It usually sits at the lower end, constrained by debt capacity, credit markets and IRR hurdles. Strategic buyers can usually pay more because of synergies.

questions.q: Banks’ credit committees require the deal team to test the target under one or more downside cases.
questions.why: Downside cases cut growth, margins and possibly cash efficiency, to check the target can still service its debt.

questions.q: The revolver’s commitment fee is charged on the amount the company has drawn down.
questions.why: It is charged on the undrawn portion. Drawn amounts pay interest at the benchmark rate plus the spread instead.

questions.q: Goodwill created in the deal equals the equity purchase price less the target’s net identifiable assets.
questions.why: Net identifiable assets are shareholders’ equity less existing goodwill. The book simplifies by allocating the whole premium to goodwill.

questions.q: The pre-LBO income statement is built all the way to net income, because the target’s existing interest costs continue.
questions.why: It is built only to EBIT. The existing debt is refinanced, so old interest is irrelevant; new interest comes from the debt schedule.

questions.q: Why is an LBO model typically projected for seven to ten years?
options: To match the maturity of the longest-dated debt in the structure
Because sponsors nearly always hold their investments for ten years
Because management projections in the CIM cover ten years
To make the IRR look higher by including more years of growth
questions.why: When a CIM gives five years, bankers often hold year-five growth and margins constant for the later years.

questions.q: Which operating case is ultimately used to set covenants and market the financing to investors?
options: The Sponsor Case
The Management Case
The Downside Case
The Upside Case
questions.why: The sponsor builds it from its own diligence. The banks check that it is feasible and that the proposed structure is marketable.

questions.q: How is cash available for debt repayment calculated in an LBO model?
options: Cash flow from operating activities plus cash flow from investing activities
EBITDA less interest expense, before any capex or working capital
Net income plus capex, since capex is added back as a non-cash item
Unlevered free cash flow from the DCF, before any interest is paid
questions.why: It is a levered free cash flow, after interest. It pays mandatory amortisation first, then optional repayments.

questions.q: In what order is excess cash usually applied to optional repayments?
options: Revolver first, then Term Loan A, then Term Loan B
Senior notes first, then the term loans, then the revolver
Term Loan B first, then Term Loan A, then the revolver
Equally across all the debt, in proportion to the balances
questions.why: Bank debt is repaid in order of seniority and prepayability; the high yield notes stay outstanding.

questions.q: In a downside case, cash available for optional repayment turns negative in one year. What does the model do?
options: Draws on the revolver or cash on hand to cover the gap, and repays it first from later surpluses
Issues new equity automatically to the sponsor, which then owns a larger share of the company
Defaults on the senior notes for that year, which the model shows as a missed coupon payment
Skips the mandatory amortisation for that year and adds it to the term loan’s final payment
questions.why: The revolver provides liquidity for exactly these periods.

questions.q: Why would a banker advising a strategic buyer run an LBO analysis?
options: To gauge what a competing sponsor could pay, and so frame the bid
Because strategic buyers usually fund deals with LBO-style financing
To calculate the synergies that the combination can be expected to deliver
To set the target’s share price before the offer is announced
questions.why: On the sell side, it also helps set price expectations for the seller.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a primary driver of the sponsor’s IRR?
options: The target’s historical share price
The purchase price
The size of the equity contribution
The exit multiple and exit year
questions.why: IRR depends on the projections, the price, the financing structure and the exit assumptions.

questions.q: The target’s existing 8% notes must be refinanced because of a change of control, and are callable at 104. How is the cost treated?
options: As a use of funds: a 4% premium on the notes, deducted from the equity contributed
As a source of funds, since the call premium is paid by the noteholders themselves
Ignored, since the notes are repaid at par when the change of control happens
Capitalised as a financing fee and amortised over the life of the new notes
questions.why: Par plus half the coupon gives 104, so the holders receive a 4% premium. Like other deal costs, it is expensed against equity.

questions.q: How did the book derive ValueCo’s LBO valuation range?
options: From entry and exit multiples giving IRRs around 20%, with equity of 25–40%
From the highest bids received in the first round of the auction process
From the DCF terminal value, discounted back at the sponsor’s target IRR
From the target’s book value, adjusted for the market value of its assets
questions.why: The sensitivity table pointed to 7.25× to 8.25× LTM EBITDA as the range.

questions.q: A private target with LTM EBITDA of R700m is bought at 8.0×. It has R1,500m of debt and R250m of cash. What are the enterprise value and equity purchase price?
options: R5,600m and R4,350m
R5,600m and R4,100m
R5,600m and R5,850m
R4,350m and R5,600m
questions.why: R700m × 8.0 = R5,600m, less net debt of R1,250m = R4,350m.

questions.q: Uses are: buy the equity for R4,350m, refinance R1,500m of debt and pay R150m of fees. Sources are a R2,150m term loan, R1,500m of notes and R250m of cash on hand. How much equity must the sponsor contribute?
questions.why: Uses total R6,000m. Debt and cash supply R3,900m, so equity = R6,000m − R3,900m = R2,100m (35%).

questions.q: The equity purchase price is R4,350m. The target’s shareholders’ equity is R3,500m, including R1,000m of existing goodwill. How much goodwill is created?
options: R850m
questions.why: Net identifiable assets = R3,500m − R1,000m = R2,500m, so goodwill = R4,350m − R2,500m = R1,850m. Old goodwill is written off.

questions.q: Fees are 1.5% on R2,400m of bank facilities, 2.25% on R1,500m of notes and 1.0% on a R1,500m bridge commitment. What do these financing fees total?
options: About R84.75m
About R54.0m
About R69.75m
About R121.5m
questions.why: R36m + R33.75m + R15m = R84.75m. The bridge fee is paid even if the bridge is never funded.

questions.q: A term loan starts the year at R2,150m and ends at R1,945m. Its rate is 5.75%. What interest does the average-balance method give?
options: About R117.7m
About R123.6m
About R111.8m
About R235.4m
questions.why: Average balance ≈ R2,047.5m, and × 5.75% ≈ R117.7m. The beginning balance alone gives R123.6m, the ending alone R111.8m.
